Summary
- PROV-O defines prov:Entity as a resource with fixed aspects (immutable for provenance), whereas real-world resources can be mutable; provenance must be unambiguous about which state an entity represents, motivating “entities as immutable foci” even as surrounding systems change off-chain <cite id="1ddea5b5-1">One of the core concepts identified by the Provenance Incubator group was that of resources, which may be immutable or mutable... it needs to be clear what state of the resource is intended... Therefore, an alternative approach was taken... prov is to model resources with fixed attributes, called entities. <cite id="1ddea5b5-3">An prov:Entity is a physical, digital, conceptual, or other kind of thing with some fixed aspects; entities may be real or imaginary.</cite> <cite id="1ddea5b5-0">In PROV... the provenance comes from the information about entities, activities, and people... PROV-O is the PROV Ontology... Three main components, prov:entity, prov:activity, and prov:agent</cite>.

- On blockchains, “immutability” is structural: blocks are appended and prior data is never changed; altering a block requires replaying the chain from a modified point, which violates collision resistance and renders the history tamper-evident but not inherently semantically consistent <cite id="a3071355-0">A blockchain is said to be immutable... any change to B_i (even a single bit) invalidates all subsequent hashlinks... Immutability is purely syntactic—it enforces structural integrity, not semantic accuracy or ethical trustworthiness of T_i</cite>. <cite id="a3071355-3">Data stored in a blockchain is considered to be immutable... blocks are only appended... data already written is never changed... The hash of the previous block must be included... However, such a blockchain still can be changed if all block hashes from a changed block onwards can be rehashed</cite>.

Which architecture violates PROV-O’s entity mutability semantics?
- On-chain PROV-O storage (writing full PROV-O graphs/updates directly into contract state) can violate PROV-O’s “fixed aspects” semantics when on-chain transactions overwrite or evolve entities/activities in the graph. Because PROV-O’s meaning hinges on unambiguous states of entities, changing an entity’s on-chain representation or creating new entities to “update” the same resource breaks the requirement that entities capture fixed aspects of a resource; future provenance that references the same identifier must not change its state <cite id="1ddea5b5-1">In referring to a mutable resource in provenance, it needs to be clear what state of the resource is intended... prov is to model resources with fixed attributes, called entities</cite>. <cite id="a3071355-3">Data already written is never changed. There is no UPDATE or DELETE.</cite> <cite id="a3071355-0">Immutability... enforces structural integrity, not semantic accuracy... even if syntactically valid, content can be incorrect or misleading</cite>. Practically, smart-contract designs that store full provenance payloads on-chain face update costs and risk semantic inconsistency when off-chain data changes, as on-chain references must remain semantically stable while the world outside evolves <cite id="a3071355-1">One of the solutions that ensures the mutability of the blockchain is to store data as off-chain storage while storing only a hash value in the blockchain... When the data stored in off-chain storage are deleted or modified, only the fact that a specific content version existed at a specific point in time is left in the blockchain</cite>.

- Off-chain provenance with hash anchoring does not violate PROV-O’s mutability semantics. Anchors commit digests and content IDs (e.g., IPFS CIDs) to chain state, binding the “fixed aspects” of a prov:Entity to an immutable on-chain reference while allowing the full RDF graph to be mutable in off-chain storage. Changes to off-chain content change the digest, making prior anchors mismatch and signaling drift; the entity identity (URI) denotes a fixed aspect baseline (e.g., the first published hash), while subsequent versions are new entities or artifacts referencing the baseline, preserving PROV-O’s state clarity and immutability of entities <cite id="a3071355-4">agent outputs are deterministically captured and hashed; the resulting hash set is stored on IPFS to generate a content identifier (CID), which is then anchored on-chain... Security relies on collision resistance... Since the hash set H is anchored on the immutable blockchain, any modification to after commitment requires finding a collision</cite>. <cite id="555a81d4-2">Payloads are stored off-chain in IPFS... CID_P and a timestamp are recorded on the Provenance Smart Contract to create an immutable link... third parties verify P’s unaltered state by recomputing the hash and checking its existence in the contract</cite>. <cite id="555a81d4-1">Recording only the Keccak-256 hash on-chain serves as a permanent, tamper-evident reference... a mismatch between a recomputed hash and the on-chain commitment signals genuine semantic drift</cite>.

Why on-chain storage can still appear attractive—and where it aligns
- Some systems argue for on-chain provenance to tightly bind facts and references to chain state, emphasizing that “on-chain provenance is critical to preserving the integrity of blockchain transactions” and that hashing/signatures keep relationships immutable. This approach can preserve semantic integrity when the entire provenance graph is committed and never mutated; however, it forfeits scalability and flexibility, and it risks violating PROV-O semantics if updates necessitate changing entities or their attributes, since such changes are effectively deletions/updates of immutable data <cite id="a3071355-2">On-chain provenance is critical to preserving the integrity of blockchain transactions... Recent work has focused on cryptographic methods such as hashing and digital signatures to verify the authenticity of recorded data... ensuring that the blockchain remains immutable while maintaining the relationship between data exchanges</cite>. <cite id="a3071355-3">There is no UPDATE or DELETE... data already written is never changed</cite>. 
- To retain W3C compliance and practicality, many designs store compact descriptors and anchors on-chain while keeping full RDF/PROV-O graphs mutable off-chain (e.g., IPFS). This is explicitly motivated by PROV-O’s need for “fixed aspects” and by blockchain costs: “Only compact hashes and metadata are stored on-chain... full data... remain off-chain.” These systems formalize verification logic so that any on-chain update that implies a change to a prov:Entity’s fixed aspects must spawn a new entity/artifact, preserving semantics and auditability <cite id="555a81d4-0">Only compact hashes and metadata are stored on-chain to minimize storage overhead, while full data... remain off-chain... structured metadata enable verifiable and gas-efficient validation</cite>. <cite id="555a81d4-2">In particular, the protocol... stores payloads off-chain in IPFS while anchoring their integrity on the blockchain</cite>. 
- Empirical systems like SlideChain and BlockA2A operationalize this: commit minimal semantic records and hashes on-chain to anchor baselines; compare recomputed hashes to detect drift, using the chain as a tamper-evident baseline rather than as a mutable graph store. This directly reflects PROV-O’s requirement that a prov:Entity’s aspects remain fixed once stated, with the chain serving as a semantic anchor rather than the locus of change <cite id="555a81d4-1">Semantic records remain off-chain... on-chain commitment serves as a permanent, tamper-evident reference... mismatch signals genuine semantic drift</cite>. <cite id="555a81d4-2">By separating storage (IPFS) from consensus (blockchain), the protocol efficiently manages large data while leveraging cryptographic guarantees</cite>. 
- There are noted downsides to off-chain anchoring: synchronization complexity, potential inconsistency, and added cost/latency, which motivate careful protocol design and validation; yet the fundamental compliance with PROV-O’s mutability is retained by keeping entities immutable/read-only behind on-chain anchors <cite id="a3071355-1">Off-chain methods... reduce the security level of the blockchain and make the system inconsistent due to data synchronization... the cost of deploying off-chain storage increases</cite>.

Title: The rationale of PROV
Snippet: One of the core concepts identified by the Provenance Incubator group was that of resources, which may be immutable or mutable (Requirement XG3). In referring to a mutable resource in provenance, it needs to be clear what state of the resource is intended. For example, consider a Web page of which there were two versions, the first including some claim and the second with the claim removed. If the provenance describes the consequences of agents reading and acting on that claim, then it should refer to the first version of the Web page and not the second, else the provenance will be nonsensical or misleading. It was also noted that the state of a resource did not just include its content, but also context, e.g. the location of the Web page. 

One possibility considered was for prov to model only immutable resources, and require each state to be separately identified (as OPM does). However, this approach was found to have a few problems. First, the provenance would still need to refer to the identified resources of which people wish to describe the provenance, e.g. a Web page identified by its URI, and these are mutable. Second, at least in some cases, it can be impractical to decide whether to model a resource as being in a new state or not, as the context of the resource can itself be defined in different ways. Finally, there are ease of use implications (discussed further in Section 7.4), as each new state requires a new identifier, which is heavyweight when a user wishes to assert a simple statement about their Web page's origins, for example. 

Therefore, an alternative approach was taken. It was noted that many changes to a resource's content or context would not have any relevance to the provenance information to be expressed. There are only certain attributes of the resource that matter, such as the presence of the claim in the Web page example above. As a first step, a requirement emerged for a concept of a resource that is immutable in certain attributes, which was termed an entity. 

Requirement RE1 (Entity). prov is to model resources with fixed attributes, called entities.

Snippet: Data stored in a blockchain is considered to be immutable. To achieve immutability, a blockchain follows these basic principles: 

1. Blocks are only appended at the end of the chain. 

2. There has to be consensus on who is allowed to append the next block to the chain in order to avoid race conditions. 

3. Data already written is never changed. There is no UPDATE or DELETE. 

4. The hash of the previous block must be included in the current block. 

The integrity of every block, and hence the whole chain, can thus be verified by comparing its hash to the predecessor hash of the following block. 

However, such a blockchain still can be changed if all block hashes from a changed block onwards can be rehashed with feasible effort. Therefore, additional safeguards are applied: 

• Copies of the blockchain are stored in multiple locations. 

• The hash function to obtain a block hash is deliberately made computationally expensive. 

• Additional attestation mechanisms, like digital signatures, can be used to further secure the block hashes.

Title: Bridging the Provenance Knowledge Gap Between 3D Digitization and Semantic Interpretation
Snippet: The PROV specification is a recognized standard in the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) dedicated for the provenance interchange on the web [57]. In PROV (Figure 5), the provenance comes from the information about entities, activities, and people involved in producing a piece of data or thing [58]. The provenance information is often used to form assessments about the quality, reliability, or trustworthiness of data. In the PROV family of models, PROV-DM is the conceptual data model that presents the core model that constitutes the foundation for the W3C Provenance (PROV) family of specifications [59]. PROV-O is the PROV Ontology, an OWL2 ontology allowing the mapping of the PROV data model to RDF [60]. Three main components, prov:entity, prov:activity, and prov:agent, express, respectively, the data flow view, the process flow, and the responsibility view.

Title: The rationale of PROV
Snippet: One of the core concepts identified by the Provenance Incubator group was that of resources, which may be immutable or mutable (Requirement XG3). In referring to a mutable resource in provenance, it needs to be clear what state of the resource is intended. For example, consider a Web page of which there were two versions, the first including some claim and the second with the claim removed. If the provenance describes the consequences of agents reading and acting on that claim, then it should refer to the first version of the Web page and not the second, else the provenance will be nonsensical or misleading. It was also noted that the state of a resource did not just include its content, but also context, e.g. the location of the Web page. 

One possibility considered was for prov to model only immutable resources, and require each state to be separately identified (as OPM does). However, this approach was found to have a few problems. First, the provenance would still need to refer to the identified resources of which people wish to describe the provenance, e.g. a Web page identified by its URI, and these are mutable. Second, at least in some cases, it can be impractical to decide whether to model a resource as being in a new state or not, as the context of the resource can itself be defined in different ways. Finally, there are ease of use implications (discussed further in Section 7.4), as each new state requires a new identifier, which is heavyweight when a user wishes to assert a simple statement about their Web page's origins, for example. 

Therefore, an alternative approach was taken. It was noted that many changes to a resource's content or context would not have any relevance to the provenance information to be expressed. There are only certain attributes of the resource that matter, such as the presence of the claim in the Web page example above. As a first step, a requirement emerged for a concept of a resource that is immutable in certain attributes, which was termed an entity. 

Requirement RE1 (Entity). prov is to model resources with fixed attributes, called entities.

Snippet: The PROV family of specifications, published by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C), is a set of provenance standard to promote provenance publication on the Web with interoperability across diverse provenance management systems [31]. One key specification is PROV-DM, an extensible relational model which describes provenance information with a graph representation. As shown in Figure 2, a W3C provenance graph abstracts information into classes of Entity, Activity, Agent, and Relation between the first three classes. Another critical specification is PROV-O which describes the mapping of PROV-DM classes to RDF triples. In PROV-O, Entity, Activity and Agent are mapped to subjects and objects, while Relation is mapped to predicates. We follow the W3C PROV standard in the PROV-IO + design.

One key specification is PROV-DM, an extensible relational model which describes provenance information with a graph representation. As shown in Figure 2, a W3C provenance graph abstracts information into classes of Entity, Activity, Agent, and Relation between the first three classes. Another critical specification is PROV-O which describes the mapping of PROV-DM classes to RDF triples. In PROV-O, Entity, Activity and Agent are mapped to subjects and objects, while Relation is mapped to predicates. We follow the W3C PROV standard in the PROV-IO + design. 

Fig. 2: The W3C Provenance Model [31].

Title: OracleTrust: A dual-layer provenance-based signature verification scheme for preventing transaction malleability in blockchain
Snippet: On-chain provenance is critical to preserving the integrity of blockchain transactions. It provides an immutable history of any data exchange. Recent work has focused on cryptographic methods such as hashing and digital signatures to verify the authenticity of recorded data. For example, a new method is presented in [13] that uses secure hashing algorithms to verify the integrity of transactions on data in decentralized networks. In the same manner, [15] developed an improved version of a blockchain-based multi-signature scheme that extends time-stamping and multi-signature techniques, ensuring that the blockchain remains immutable while maintaining the relationship between data exchanges. However, even with the recent developments, scalability remains a problem, particularly in low-volume applications such as the Internet of Things (IoT) networks [16,17]. The development of blockchain oracles is increasingly influenced by the architectural and philosophical differences between major blockchain ecosystems. Although Ethereum defined the initial model of smart contract-interconnected oracles, new networks, such as Polkadot, Cardano, and Solana, have developed their own models of scalability, consensus, and interoperability, each with its own oracle systems. These architectural differences affect the design trade-offs and the security vulnerability of the oracle networks, especially on transaction malleability, data integrity, and cross-chain data validation.

Title: Right to Sign: Safeguarding data immutability in blockchain systems with cryptographic signatures over a broad range of available consensus finding scenarios
Snippet: Data stored in a blockchain is considered to be immutable. To achieve immutability, a blockchain follows these basic principles: 

1. Blocks are only appended at the end of the chain. 

2. There has to be consensus on who is allowed to append the next block to the chain in order to avoid race conditions. 

3. Data already written is never changed. There is no UPDATE or DELETE. 

4. The hash of the previous block must be included in the current block. 

The integrity of every block, and hence the whole chain, can thus be verified by comparing its hash to the predecessor hash of the following block. 

However, such a blockchain still can be changed if all block hashes from a changed block onwards can be rehashed with feasible effort. Therefore, additional safeguards are applied: 

• Copies of the blockchain are stored in multiple locations. 

• The hash function to obtain a block hash is deliberately made computationally expensive. 

• Additional attestation mechanisms, like digital signatures, can be used to further secure the block hashes.

Title: Trustworthy AI for secure and robust machine learning through blockchain enabled data integrity
Snippet: A permissioned blockchain smart contract governs provenance registration, update verification, and model versioning. Only compact hashes and metadata are stored on-chain to minimize storage overhead, while full data and gradients remain off-chain. 

Three transaction types are defined: PROVENANCE_REG, UPDATE_SUBMIT, and MODEL_PUBLISH. Each transaction includes digital signatures, Merkle root references, and structured metadata to enable verifiable and gas-efficient validation. 

Pseudocode for critical smart contract functions is provided to formalize the verification logic. 

On-chain objects (compact): 

• PROVENANCE_REG: client_id, merkle_root, dataset_size, timestamp, sig, offchain_uri 

Storage strategy: Store only fixed-size hashes and small metadata fields. Use off-chain storage (IPFS or secure institutional storage) for actual sample content and full gradient payloads. For public chains where gas is expensive, further compress metadata and batch multiple digests into a single transaction using Merkle-of-digests patterns.

Title: SlideChain: Semantic Provenance for Lecture Understanding via Blockchain Registration
Snippet: To clarify why SlideChain adopts a blockchain-backed provenance layer rather than conventional version control or logging mechanisms, Table 4 contrasts these approaches along key integrity and trust dimensions. From a systems perspective, SlideChain demonstrates that blockchain-backed provenance can provide strong integrity guarantees with minimal overhead. The smart contract exhibits nearly constant gas usage per slide registration, confirming that the design remains lightweight even when applied to full-course datasets. Recording only the Keccak-256 hash onchain strikes a deliberate balance: semantic records remain off-chain for flexibility and scalability, while the on-chain commitment serves as a permanent, tamper-evident reference. 

Reproducibility experiments further emphasize this role. Under fixed prompts and execution environments, repeated extraction runs produce identical provenance records. Any future mismatch between a recomputed hash and the on-chain commitment therefore signals genuine semantic drift-whether due to model updates, preprocessing changes, or unintended modification. In this sense, SlideChain functions as a stability anchor, preserving a canonical semantic baseline against which future interpretations can be audited. 

Such auditability is particularly important in educational settings, where lecture materials evolve, courses are revised, and AI models are continually updated. Provenance ensures that semantic interpretations remain reviewable, accountable, and historically traceable across these changes.

Title: BlockA2A: Towards Secure and Verifiable Agent-to-Agent Interoperability
Snippet: The Data Anchoring Protocol (Protocol 8) extends the decentralized provenance framework established by the Task Initiation and State Transition Validation Protocols, providing the infrastructure to ensure long-term integrity for large data payloads (e.g., contracts, audit logs). In particular, the protocol addresses scalability by storing payloads off-chain in IPFS while anchoring their integrity on the blockchain. The workflow begins with the data owner hashing the payload (P ) using SHA-256 to generate H P , mirroring the hash computation in task initiation. The payload is then stored on IPFS, yielding a content identifier (CID P ) that uniquely maps to P 's content. Both H P , CID P , and a timestamp (t) are recorded on the Provenance Smart Contract-reusing the same contract infrastructure as prior protocols-to create an immutable link between the off-chain data and its on-chain proof. This allows third parties to verify P 's unaltered state at any time by recomputing H P and checking its existence in the contract, aligning with the multi-signature verification logic in Protocol 7. By separating storage (IPFS) from consensus (blockchain), the protocol efficiently manages large data while leveraging cryptographic guarantees. This design integrates seamlessly with task lifecycles: for example, a milestone in Protocol 7 might reference an anchored dataset, ensuring all stakeholders act on verifiably consistent information.

Title: StorjLedger: An Innovative Distributed Storage Ecosystem That Overcomes Blockchain Trade‐Offs Using Erasure‐Coded Sharding and Proof‐of‐Storage Consensus
Snippet: The Anchor Chain serves as StorjLedger's immutable ledger for cryptographic metadata, anchoring shard locations, Merkle roots, and audit logs in 64-byte blocks. Unlike conventional blockchains storing full data, it cryptographically links off-chain shards to on-chain verification parameters (BLAKE2b-512 hashes). This design ensures: 

-Tamper-Proof Traceability: Shard metadata is irreversibly logged, enabling Byzantine-resilient retrieval. 

-Scalability: 85.7% smaller than Bitcoin's transactions. 

-Integrity Checks: Validators cross-reference Sparse Merkle Tree roots against Anchor Chain records during audits. 

Figure 2 highlights its centrality in the workflow.

Title: Research and Application of data provenance based on PROV
Snippet: PROV-O means PROV Ontology, which defines the OWL2 Web Ontology Language encoding of the PROV Data Model. Elements of PROV-O is corresponding to PROV-DM, mainly including the set of classes, properties, and restrictions that constitute the PROV Ontology. PROV Ontology provides the foundation to implement provenance applications in different domains, which can reproduce, exchange, and integrate provenance information generated in heterogeneous systems or under different contexts. We can know in chapter 2 that PROV-DM defines how to describe provenance information and sets up a generic conception model to represent provenance information in a variety of application domains. snippet.text:
A permissioned blockchain smart contract governs provenance registration, update verification, and model versioning. Only compact hashes and metadata are stored on-chain to minimize storage overhead, while full data and gradients remain off-chain. 

Three transaction types are defined: PROVENANCE_REG, UPDATE_SUBMIT, and MODEL_PUBLISH. Each transaction includes digital signatures, Merkle root references, and structured metadata to enable verifiable and gas-efficient validation. 

Pseudocode for critical smart contract functions is provided to formalize the verification logic. 

On-chain objects (compact): 

• PROVENANCE_REG: client_id, merkle_root, dataset_size, timestamp, sig, offchain_uri 

Storage strategy: Store only fixed-size hashes and small metadata fields. Use off-chain storage (IPFS or secure institutional storage) for actual sample content and full gradient payloads. For public chains where gas is expensive, further compress metadata and batch multiple digests into a single transaction using Merkle-of-digests patterns.

snippet.text:
To clarify why SlideChain adopts a blockchain-backed provenance layer rather than conventional version control or logging mechanisms, Table 4 contrasts these approaches along key integrity and trust dimensions. From a systems perspective, SlideChain demonstrates that blockchain-backed provenance can provide strong integrity guarantees with minimal overhead. The smart contract exhibits nearly constant gas usage per slide registration, confirming that the design remains lightweight even when applied to full-course datasets. Recording only the Keccak-256 hash onchain strikes a deliberate balance: semantic records remain off-chain for flexibility and scalability, while the on-chain commitment serves as a permanent, tamper-evident reference. 

Reproducibility experiments further emphasize this role. Under fixed prompts and execution environments, repeated extraction runs produce identical provenance records. Any future mismatch between a recomputed hash and the on-chain commitment therefore signals genuine semantic drift-whether due to model updates, preprocessing changes, or unintended modification. In this sense, SlideChain functions as a stability anchor, preserving a canonical semantic baseline against which future interpretations can be audited. 

Such auditability is particularly important in educational settings, where lecture materials evolve, courses are revised, and AI models are continually updated. Provenance ensures that semantic interpretations remain reviewable, accountable, and historically traceable across these changes.

snippet.text: The Data Anchoring Protocol (Protocol 8) extends the decentralized provenance framework established by the Task Initiation and State Transition Validation Protocols, providing the infrastructure to ensure long-term integrity for large data payloads (e.g., contracts, audit logs). In particular, the protocol addresses scalability by storing payloads off-chain in IPFS while anchoring their integrity on the blockchain. The workflow begins with the data owner hashing the payload (P ) using SHA-256 to generate H P , mirroring the hash computation in task initiation. The payload is then stored on IPFS, yielding a content identifier (CID P ) that uniquely maps to P 's content. Both H P , CID P , and a timestamp (t) are recorded on the Provenance Smart Contract-reusing the same contract infrastructure as prior protocols-to create an immutable link between the off-chain data and its on-chain proof. This allows third parties to verify P 's unaltered state at any time by recomputing H P and checking its existence in the contract, aligning with the multi-signature verification logic in Protocol 7. By separating storage (IPFS) from consensus (blockchain), the protocol efficiently manages large data while leveraging cryptographic guarantees. This design integrates seamlessly with task lifecycles: for example, a milestone in Protocol 7 might reference an anchored dataset, ensuring all stakeholders act on verifiably consistent information.

-Integrity Checks: Validators cross-reference Sparse Merkle Tree roots against Anchor Chain records during audits.

judgment.criterion_reasoning: The answer explicitly identifies on-chain storage as violating PROV-O's entity mutability semantics. It states: 'On-chain PROV-O storage (writing full PROV-O graphs/updates directly into contract state) can violate PROV-O's "fixed aspects" semantics when on-chain transactions overwrite or evolve entities/activities in the graph.' The answer explains that PROV-O requires entities to capture fixed aspects of a resource, but on-chain updates that change entity representations break this requirement. It cites Reference [1] which describes PROV-O's requirement RE1 for 'resources with fixed attributes, called entities' and notes that 'it needs to be clear what state of the resource is intended' to avoid 'nonsensical or misleading' provenance. The answer further explains that PROV-O entities must remain semantically stable (fixed aspects cannot change), whereas blockchain's structural immutability cannot prevent semantic violations when on-chain graphs are mutated. It contrasts this with off-chain anchoring, which preserves PROV-O semantics by anchoring fixed aspects as hashes while allowing content to evolve off-chain.
other_issues: Conceptual confusion: The answer conflates two distinct meanings of 'mutability.' PROV-O entities are actually immutable by design (they represent fixed aspects), but the answer frames this as 'entity mutability semantics' in the question and throughout. The real issue is that PROV-O allows *adding* new provenance statements about existing entities (incremental extension/growth of the provenance graph), not mutating entity properties themselves.

Misleading framing: The answer states 'PROV-O allows entities to gain new properties/relationships' in the verification criterion description is not clearly demonstrated. Instead, Reference [1] emphasizes that entities have 'fixed attributes' - the mutability discussion concerns the underlying *resource*, not the entity. The answer doesn't clearly distinguish between resource mutability and entity immutability.

The answer correctly identifies on-chain storage as problematic but for somewhat muddled reasons - it focuses on 'changing entities' when the real semantic issue is that blockchain prevents adding new provenance statements that reference past entity states without creating entirely new blocks, making incremental provenance extension cumbersome.

Reference [1] is correctly cited and relevant, establishing that PROV-O entities must have 'fixed attributes' and that changes to underlying resources require clarity about which state is being described.
judgment.summary: The answer satisfies the verification criterion by identifying on-chain storage as violating PROV-O semantics and citing appropriate evidence from Reference [1] about entity fixed aspects. However, it exhibits conceptual confusion about what 'entity mutability' means in PROV-O - entities are immutable by design, but the provenance graph can grow incrementally. The answer conflates resource mutability with entity mutability, though it still arrives at the correct architectural conclusion about on-chain vs. off-chain storage.

The judge noted conceptual confusion about entity vs. graph-level mutability, but the system still arrived at the correct answer. To make this harder, I need to avoid straightforward architectural comparisons. Options: (1) Require reasoning about temporal coherence when PROV-O's open-world assumption conflicts with blockchain's closed-block finality; (2) Require identifying a subtle circular dependency in cross-chain provenance verification where hash-based anchoring undermines PROV-O's trust model; (3) Require reasoning about whether decentralized PROV-O queries can achieve completeness guarantees when provenance fragments are sharded across blockchain nodes with eventual consistency. attempts.answer:
Below is an evidence-backed explanation of how “hash‑anchored” PROV‑O provenance verification can create a bootstrapping paradox for cross‑chain entity derivation claims.

Summary and context
- PROV‑O makes provenance first‑class in RDF/OWL: entities, activities, and derivation relations (e.g., prov:wasDerivedFrom) are modeled as OWL classes and properties, enabling fine‑grained, auditable lineage and qualified attribution across systems and vocabularies.<cite id="c68639c1-0">Following the PROV‑O model, the provenance of an entity is either an entity or an activity, with hierarchical propagation of provenance for structured objects</cite><cite id="c68639c1-3">Systems such as Europeana/EDM, Google Data Commons, Bio2RDF, Wikidata, and FHIR adopt PROV‑O to capture dataset/entity lineage, agent roles, and triple‑level provenance as first‑class model elements</cite><cite id="fd82574d-1">PROV‑O expresses PROV entities/relationships in OWL, with primary provenance classes (entities, activities, agents) and derivation/attribution relations</cite><cite id="fd82574d-4">PROV‑O provides standard terms for tracing origin and derivation history, including prov:wasDerivedFrom and prov:wasAttributedTo, and can be extended for domain‑specific provenance</cite>. 
- “Hash‑anchored” verification ties provenance or data to cryptographic roots stored in trusted substrates (e.g., blockchains, TEEs, logs) so verifiers can cheaply check integrity without full re‑computation.<cite id="03fdbce3-0">Merkle roots and hash chains provide end‑to‑end provenance verification; for complex pipelines, a semantic layer like RDF/PROV adds granularity, while Merkle roots offer efficient verification</cite><cite id="4a7ee33b-4">BlockA2A anchors large payloads off‑chain (IPFS) by recording SHA‑256 hashes, CID, and a timestamp on a provenance smart contract, enabling third‑party constant‑cost verification by recomputing the hash and checking contract‑bound proofs</cite><cite id="05239b10-1">Hash‑chain/external‑anchor patterns from software attestation and blockchain auditing are used to bind artifacts to external anchors (e.g., transparency logs/timestamping authorities)</cite>. 
- Cross‑chain entity derivation is commonly implemented by composing PROV‑O derivation relations and qualified attribution across chains, with cryptographic anchors serving as cross‑substrate integrity witnesses for entity identity/equivalence claims.<cite id="fd82574d-2">Directed provenance graphs model traceable entities across a chain with derivation edges supporting trace‑back/trace‑forward reasoning</cite><cite id="c68639c1-3">Open data/EDM and FHIR use PROV‑O qualified attribution and lineage to map entities across providers and aggregators</cite><cite id="4a7ee33b-4">Anchored contracts link off‑chain payloads to on‑chain proofs, enabling third parties to verify a dataset’s unaltered state and to anchor downstream provenance</cite>.

How hash‑anchored PROV‑O verification is put together
- Anchored provenance graphs. A common design is to publish RDF/PROV documents or pointers within them, alongside cryptographic anchors (hashes, Merkle roots) committed to a trusted store; verifiers recompute hashes and check against anchors to validate subgraphs or entire entities.<cite id="03fdbce3-0">Merkle root and hash‑chain verification end‑to‑end; semantic layers add granularity for multi‑step processes</cite><cite id="4a7ee33b-4">Workflow: hash the payload, store in IPFS (CID), record (hash, CID, timestamp) on a provenance smart contract; verifiers recompute hash and check contract to confirm existence and integrity</cite><cite id="05239b10-1">External anchors (e.g., logs and timestamp services) complement hash‑chains to provide independent commitment points</cite>. 
- Trust chains and chain‑of‑custody. In assured execution settings, “chains of provenance” of service identities are carried end‑to‑end; each link is a cryptographic hash of the next service, enabling verifiers to retrace back to a root anchor and confirm custody and transformation provenance.<cite id="4a7ee33b-1">Trust chains are lists of service hashes; services verify code hash and source hash, and extend chains by pushing the recipient’s hash to the front; observers can trace back to the anchoring program</cite>. 
- Cross‑chain derivation claims. A cross‑chain claim that entity B on chain 2 derives from (or is equivalent to) entity A on chain 1 is asserted via PROV‑O relations (e.g., prov:wasDerivedFrom, prov:quotation, prov:association) and supported by anchored proofs: either the entities’ internal Merkle roots or their enclosing provenance document anchors.<cite id="fd82574d-2">Derivation edges (u, v) mean v is produced using or contains u, enabling upstream/downstream reasoning across a chain</cite><cite id="c68639c1-3">Qualified attribution and lineage (prov:qualifiedAttribution, prov:association) connect datasets and agents across providers and aggregators</cite><cite id="4a7ee33b-4">Anchored datasets can be referenced in task lifecycles so stakeholders act on verifiably consistent information</cite>.

Why this creates a bootstrapping paradox
Bootstrapping paradox (circularity) emerges when the truth of cross‑chain derivation claims depends on anchored cryptographic witnesses whose trust derivations, in turn, rely on the same cross‑chain provenance story. Three mechanisms make this loop concrete.
1) Mutual anchoring: derivation claims anchor data, while anchors are interpreted through derivation claims

Snippet: In this work, we have used cryptographic tools such as hashing and Merkle root with the help of MultiChain blockchain to verify end-to-end provenance of a stream processing result. Title: Knowledge Graph Re-engineering Along the Ontological Continuum (extended version)
Snippet: Europeana uses the Europeana Data Model (EDM), capturing provenance through OAI-ORE Aggregations that record the original data provider, intermediaries, and Europeana as aggregator, with Dublin Core metadata at the core [26]. 

Google Data Commons extends Schema.org to attach a provenance property to every triple, recording the originating provider's URL as a first-class element of the data model [20,23]. 

Bio2RDF stores per-dataset provenance in dedicated named graphs, using VoID, PROV, and Dublin Core to describe conversion dates, licensing, and generating scripts [6]. 

The British Museum ResearchSpace platform uses RDF reification grounded in CIDOC-CRM to capture the provenance of scholarly assertions about cultural heritage objects [48]. 

UniProt has adopted RDF-Star to attach evidence and provenance annotations to individual triples, replacing a verbose and costly reification-based approach [25,49]. 

Wikidata provides fine-grained triple-level provenance through a bespoke statement model of qualifiers and references [51,28]. 

The EU Open Data Portal captures dataset provenance through DCAT-AP, incorporating PROV-O via prov:qualifiedAttribution to express agent roles and data lineage [31,14]. 

DBpedia organises Wikipedia-extracted data into named graphs per language and dataset, using PROV-O to record extraction process and originating source [2]. 

Linked Open Vocabularies (LOV) tracks vocabulary publication provenance using PROV-O, recording authors, publishers, versioning history, and curation agents [50]. 

Nanopublications treat provenance as a structural concern: each nanopublication comprises three named graphs: assertion, provenance, and publication info, with PROV-O capturing authorship, temporal data, and the epistemic status of scientific claims [21]. 

The ten KGs span the continuum along all four dimensions (see Table 1). The feature vocabulary is derived empirically during the analysis, reusing terms across KGs for consistency, not from a pre-existing controlled vocabulary.

Title: QCIVET: A Quantum-Classical Pipeline Integrity Framework with Contract-Based Subtype Verification and Hash-Chained Audit Traces
Snippet: The state of the art for classical pipelines is built around attested provenance. in-toto [47] formalises a "farm-to-table" chain of attestations linking sources to artefacts; SLSA [43] layers a maturity model on top, with active analysis of adoption challenges [44]; Sigstore [33] offers keyless signing and a public transparency log. Recent work [35] systematises provenance, tamper resistance, and build integrity practices across this ecosystem. Closely related, hash-chain-based integrity verification has been used in adjacent domains [18,23,40], notably blockchain transaction auditing, and QCIVET inherits the chain-of-commitments idea from this line. 

These tools assume that the artefact under attestation is a binary, image, or package whose integrity is fully captured by a cryptographic hash of its bytes. This assumption holds for classical software but breaks for the quantum stages of a hybrid pipeline in two distinct ways. First, hardware noise: the same quantum circuit, when executed on a real QPU, can produce different outputs depending on the calibration drift and the prevailing single-and two-qubit error rates. Second, semantic substitution: a byte-level-conformant "sneaky" circuit (formally characterised in Section 5) may pass a weak observable contract while violating an informationally complete one. Two artefacts with identical hashes can therefore exhibit very different quantum behaviours. QCIVET inherits the hash-chain and external-anchor pattern from this literature (Sigstore Rekor and RFC 3161 [1] timestamping authorities are concrete instantiations of our ExternalAnchor interface) and extends it with an observable-deviation check at each quantum stage. Table 1 contrasts these classical supply-chain tools with QCIVET on three dimensions: hash-chain integrity, external anchoring, and quantum-stage scope. 

Table 1: Classical supply-chain integrity versus QCIVET.
</snippet>

Each query location in Q corresponds to a consistency check between claimed sources and derived conclusions. By the PCP theorem, polynomial-size proofs can be verified with O(1) queries. Title: Immutability Does Not Guarantee Trust: A Formal and Logical Refutation
Snippet: To rigorously dismantle the belief that immutability guarantees trust, we now construct formal counterexamples demonstrating their non-equivalence. These counterexamples do not merely refute the claim empirically; they expose its logical invalidity by constructing admissible models where immutability holds but rational trust does not follow. Each example is designed to isolate one of the flawed inferential steps commonly found in popular blockchain discourse. By formalising the conditions under which trust predicates fail to arise despite perfect immutability, we expose the category mistake that underlies this belief. The epistemic assumptions ascribed to structural properties are ungrounded. Immutability, as defined by hash-linked data integrity, is a mechanical constraint on alteration-not a guarantee of semantic content, ethical provenance, predictive validity, or system benevolence. 

What follows are illustrative constructions: a predictive fraud mechanism exploiting deterministic inclusion, and a pathological data inclusion scenario we term "garbage permanence." These cases instantiate models where Immutable(B) holds under cryptographic rigor, yet Trust A (B) is either irrational or unsound by predicate logic. This reveals a critical fissure between system design properties and user belief rationality-a fissure that must be explicitly acknowledged and never papered over by rhetorical analogy.

PROV-O [3], an OWL ontology developed by the W3C Provenance Working group [13] aims to provide a standard for representing and exchanging domainindependent provenance information between applications and systems. PROV-O provides terms that can be used to trace the origin of a given resource, its derivation history, as well as the relationship between the resources, and the entities that contributed to the existence of the resource. Below is an evidence-backed explanation of how “hash‑anchored” PROV‑O provenance verification can create a bootstrapping paradox for cross‑chain entity derivation claims.

Summary and context
- PROV‑O makes provenance first‑class in RDF/OWL: entities, activities, and derivation relations (e.g., prov:wasDerivedFrom) are modeled as OWL classes and properties, enabling fine‑grained, auditable lineage and qualified attribution across systems and vocabularies.<cite id="c68639c1-0">Following the PROV‑O model, the provenance of an entity is either an entity or an activity, with hierarchical propagation of provenance for structured objects</cite><cite id="c68639c1-3">Systems such as Europeana/EDM, Google Data Commons, Bio2RDF, Wikidata, and FHIR adopt PROV‑O to capture dataset/entity lineage, agent roles, and triple‑level provenance as first‑class model elements</cite><cite id="fd82574d-1">PROV‑O expresses PROV entities/relationships in OWL, with primary provenance classes (entities, activities, agents) and derivation/attribution relations</cite><cite id="fd82574d-4">PROV‑O provides standard terms for tracing origin and derivation history, including prov:wasDerivedFrom and prov:wasAttributedTo, and can be extended for domain‑specific provenance</cite>. 
- “Hash‑anchored” verification ties provenance or data to cryptographic roots stored in trusted substrates (e.g., blockchains, TEEs, logs) so verifiers can cheaply check integrity without full re‑computation.<cite id="03fdbce3-0">Merkle roots and hash chains provide end‑to‑end provenance verification; for complex pipelines, a semantic layer like RDF/PROV adds granularity, while Merkle roots offer efficient verification</cite><cite id="4a7ee33b-4">BlockA2A anchors large payloads off‑chain (IPFS) by recording SHA‑256 hashes, CID, and a timestamp on a provenance smart contract, enabling third‑party constant‑cost verification by recomputing the hash and checking contract‑bound proofs</cite><cite id="05239b10-1">Hash‑chain/external‑anchor patterns from software attestation and blockchain auditing are used to bind artifacts to external anchors (e.g., transparency logs/timestamping authorities)</cite>. 
- Cross‑chain entity derivation is commonly implemented by composing PROV‑O derivation relations and qualified attribution across chains, with cryptographic anchors serving as cross‑substrate integrity witnesses for entity identity/equivalence claims.<cite id="fd82574d-2">Directed provenance graphs model traceable entities across a chain with derivation edges supporting trace‑back/trace‑forward reasoning</cite><cite id="c68639c1-3">Open data/EDM and FHIR use PROV‑O qualified attribution and lineage to map entities across providers and aggregators</cite><cite id="4a7ee33b-4">Anchored contracts link off‑chain payloads to on‑chain proofs, enabling third parties to verify a dataset’s unaltered state and to anchor downstream provenance</cite>.

How hash‑anchored PROV‑O verification is put together
- Anchored provenance graphs. A common design is to publish RDF/PROV documents or pointers within them, alongside cryptographic anchors (hashes, Merkle roots) committed to a trusted store; verifiers recompute hashes and check against anchors to validate subgraphs or entire entities.<cite id="03fdbce3-0">Merkle root and hash‑chain verification end‑to‑end; semantic layers add granularity for multi‑step processes</cite><cite id="4a7ee33b-4">Workflow: hash the payload, store in IPFS (CID), record (hash, CID, timestamp) on a provenance smart contract; verifiers recompute hash and check contract to confirm existence and integrity</cite><cite id="05239b10-1">External anchors (e.g., logs and timestamp services) complement hash‑chains to provide independent commitment points</cite>. 
- Trust chains and chain‑of‑custody. In assured execution settings, “chains of provenance” of service identities are carried end‑to‑end; each link is a cryptographic hash of the next service, enabling verifiers to retrace back to a root anchor and confirm custody and transformation provenance.<cite id="4a7ee33b-1">Trust chains are lists of service hashes; services verify code hash and source hash, and extend chains by pushing the recipient’s hash to the front; observers can trace back to the anchoring program</cite>. 
- Cross‑chain derivation claims. A cross‑chain claim that entity B on chain 2 derives from (or is equivalent to) entity A on chain 1 is asserted via PROV‑O relations (e.g., prov:wasDerivedFrom, prov:quotation, prov:association) and supported by anchored proofs: either the entities’ internal Merkle roots or their enclosing provenance document anchors.<cite id="fd82574d-2">Derivation edges (u, v) mean v is produced using or contains u, enabling upstream/downstream reasoning across a chain</cite><cite id="c68639c1-3">Qualified attribution and lineage (prov:qualifiedAttribution, prov:association) connect datasets and agents across providers and aggregators</cite><cite id="4a7ee33b-4">Anchored datasets can be referenced in task lifecycles so stakeholders act on verifiably consistent information</cite>.

Why this creates a bootstrapping paradox
Bootstrapping paradox (circularity) emerges when the truth of cross‑chain derivation claims depends on anchored cryptographic witnesses whose trust derivations, in turn, rely on the same cross‑chain provenance story. Three mechanisms make this loop concrete.
1) Mutual anchoring: derivation claims anchor data, while anchors are interpreted through derivation claims
- When a cross‑chain claim states “B was derived from A,” verifiers typically check that B’s content or enclosing provenance hash matches A’s lineage digest. But the meaning and scope of the hash (what content it covers, what transformations are trusted) are defined by PROV‑O statements and associated policies, which may themselves cite cross‑chain entities or contracts as primary sources. This yields a loop: the anchor validates bytes; the PROV graph validates derivation; but the graph’s semantics depend on the anchor‑bound entities to be first‑class evidence of identity/equivalence, creating a self‑fulfilling loop.<cite id="03fdbce3-0">Merkle root/hashes guarantee integrity but “don’t explain any meaning”; a semantic layer (RDF/PROV) is added to tie steps to meaningful derivation</cite><cite id="4a7ee33b-4">On‑chain anchors bind off‑chain content identifiers and timestamps, enabling third‑party verification that aligns with multi‑signature contract logic and lifecycle references</cite><cite id="fd82574d-2">Derivation edges formalize that downstream entities are produced using upstream ones, supporting trace‑back/forward reasoning</cite>.

- In trust‑chain designs, each service extends a chain by pushing the recipient’s hash to the front, enabling verification back to an anchor. If an intermediate link is a cross‑chain provenance assertion (e.g., a contract/service that produced the next chain segment by interpreting PROV‑O), then the link’s validity depends on the semantics of PROV‑O across chains. 3) First‑class provenance and qualified attribution make the anchor content‑dependent
- PROV‑O treats provenance as first‑class and allows qualification by agents, tools, and processes. Cross‑chain claims therefore often include provenance‑level statements (who derived what, with what tools) that are themselves anchored. If the anchor’s digest includes or references those provenance statements, then the anchor both validates and defines the scope of the derivation claim, making the claim’s truth partly a function of itself being anchored, i.e., a bootstrapping loop.<cite id="c68639c1-0">In PROV‑O, provenance can be an entity or activity (e.g., external process or computational process), and provenance propagates hierarchically</cite><cite id="c68639c1-3">Open‑data and FHIR integrations use PROV‑O qualified attribution and lineage as first‑class model elements to connect providers and aggregators</cite><cite id="4a7ee33b-4">Contracts tie content hashes and timestamps to datasets, allowing downstream stakeholders to verify consistent information</cite>.

Operational mechanics of the paradox in cross‑chain verification
- Anchor as evidence, evidence as anchor. Verifiers check a cross‑chain claim by confirming that the target entity’s content hash or document anchor matches the lineage digest published for the source entity. But the lineage digest is computed over PROV‑O statements that assert derivation, attribution, and equivalence across chains; those statements are themselves anchored (e.g., committed to a smart contract or TEE). Thus, the claim’s acceptance depends on anchored statements whose anchoring depends on the claim’s semantics, creating a mutual reinforcement loop.<cite id="03fdbce3-0">Hashes/Merkle roots verify integrity but require a semantic layer to explain meaning; RDF/PROV adds step‑level semantics for multi‑step processes</cite><cite id="4a7ee33b-4">Hash + CID + timestamp recorded on contract creates an immutable link between off‑chain data and on‑chain proof; verifiers recompute hash and check existence in the contract</cite><cite id="fd82574d-4">PROV‑O provides prov:wasDerivedFrom and prov:wasAttributedTo, enabling process‑level and high‑level entity‑entity and entity‑agent relations</cite>. 
- Interpretation asymmetry and adversarial leverage. Because byte‑level equality can be decoupled from semantic equivalence, malicious actors can craft “hash‑aligned but semantically wrong” cross‑chain derivations if anchor verification is not coupled to semantic checks. Formal analyses show that while constant‑work spot‑checks suffice under cryptographic binding, adversarial populations can force quadratic work to detect inconsistencies, and naive hash checks can pass semantically invalid claims; without explicit semantic validation aligned with PROV‑O, bootstrapped anchors can be gamed.<cite id="05239b10-2">Merkle tree commitments with redundancy‑encoded provenance graphs enable constant‑work verification via O(1) spot‑checks under cryptographic binding; however, adversarial populations hiding Θ(n) sources require Ω(n²) cross‑source comparisons to detect inconsistencies</cite><cite id="05239b10-4">Immutability of hash‑linked data does not guarantee trust; pathological inclusions (“garbage permanence”) and semantic substitution can persist under cryptographic rigor, exposing a category error in equating immutability with trust</cite><cite id="05239b10-1">Byte‑level conformity can be misleading in hybrid pipelines; external anchors and observable‑deviation checks are needed beyond hash‑chains</cite>. 
- Trust graph closure. As bootstrapping iteratively promotes inferred links between chains (e.g., by hash collisions), the closure of the PROV‑O derivation graph increasingly depends on anchored edges that were justified by the same bootstrapping process. The result is a circularly closed trust web: entities become “trusted” because they are anchored, and anchors become “meaningful” because the PROV graph says so; verification succeeds only within a self‑contained closure that is hard to challenge from outside.<cite id="4a7ee33b-0">Bootstrapping starts from a seed set and grows anchors by proposing link candidates via nearest‑neighbor hash matches and promoting high‑confidence links as new anchors</cite><cite id="fd82574d-2">Derivation graphs support trace‑back/forward reasoning; downstream entities inherit upstream properties, reinforcing closed chains</cite>.

Implications and mitigations
- Make anchoring explicit and first‑class in PROV‑O graphs. Treat anchors (hashes, contracts, TEE attestations) as PROV entities/activities with clear provenance properties (prov:wasDerivedFrom, prov:used, prov:hadPrimarySource) and attach agent/role statements. This separates “what is anchored” from “what it is used to prove,” reducing circular self‑justification.<cite id="fd82574d-4">PROV‑O provides derivation and attribution relations and can be extended for domain‑specific provenance, enabling explicit modeling of primary sources and quotations</cite><cite id="c68639c1-3">Qualified attribution and lineage as first‑class model elements connect agents, processes, and datasets across aggregations</cite>. 
- Couple hash checks with semantic validation and policy signatures. Use on‑chain/off‑chain policies and attestations (e.g., signatures, zero‑knowledge proofs, observable‑level checks) to validate that the semantics asserted by PROV‑O align with the anchored bytes; this breaks pure byte‑hash loops and limits adversarial substitution.<cite id="05239b10-1">Beyond hash‑chains, external anchors (logs, timestamping) and observable‑deviation checks are needed to capture semantics and guard against sneaky artefacts</cite><cite id="05239b10-2">Cryptographic binding with redundancy‑encoded provenance graphs enables constant‑work spot‑checks and strong soundness when attackers lack committed provenance</cite>. 
- Separate storage and commitment with verifiable provenance graphs. Store large payloads off‑chain and anchor compact proofs on‑chain; have cross‑chain derivation claims reference the anchored proofs rather than embedding large content. This constrains what can be circularly justified and enables independent revalidation of the claim’s semantic structure.<cite id="4a7ee33b-4">Hash anchoring to contracts links off‑chain content to on‑chain proofs; verifiers recompute hashes and check contract‑bound existence and timestamps</cite><cite id="03fdbce3-0">Merkle roots reduce verification cost and, combined with semantic layers, provide both integrity and step‑level meaning</cite>. 
- Use chain‑of‑custody provenance to ground trust in observed transformations. Maintain trust chains of services that process and attest provenance, with each step’s hash binding to the next; by anchoring service identity and transformation provenance, cross‑chain derivation claims can cite these attested chains rather than bootstrapping equivalence directly from noisy hash collisions.<cite id="4a7ee33b-1">Trust chains carry service hashes and allow observers to trace back to the anchoring program by verifying each link’s code and source hash</cite><cite id="fd82574d-2">Derivation edges formalize production/containment relations, enabling trace‑back/forward reasoning through transformations</cite>. 
- Auditability and cost/complexity awareness. Because verification work depends on how proofs are structured and how much adversarial censorship is tolerated, design for constant‑work proofs and independent checkpoints. This limits the verifier’s exposure to circularly anchored subsets and makes bootstrapping loops easier to detect and bound.<cite id="05239b10-2">Under cryptographic hardness, constant‑work verification is possible with soundness 2⁻ᵏ; adversarial censorship forces quadratic work to detect inconsistencies without committed provenance</cite>.

Takeaway
- Hash‑anchored PROV‑O cross‑chain verification is powerful: it binds semantic lineage to cryptographic roots and enables scalable, auditable cross‑substrate claims.<cite id="03fdbce3-0">Hashes/Merkle roots efficiently verify integrity; PROV adds meaningful step‑level semantics</cite><cite id="4a7ee33b-4">Contracts anchor content hashes and timestamps for third‑party verification across chains</cite>. 
- The bootstrapping paradox arises when derivation claims depend on anchors whose semantics are defined by the same cross‑chain provenance, and when iterative anchor promotion closes the loop by treating inferred links as first‑class anchors. This yields mutual reinforcement and potential semantic brittleness or adversarial abuse if uncoupled from explicit policy and semantic checks.<cite id="4a7ee33b-0">Iterative bootstrapping promotes inferred links between anchors, growing the trusted set from seed collisions</cite><cite id="05239b10-4">Immutability alone does not guarantee trust; pathological inclusion and semantic mismatches can persist</cite><cite id="05239b10-1">External anchors and observable checks are needed to prevent semantically invalid but hash‑conformant claims</cite>. 
- Practically, keep anchoring explicit, validate semantics and policies alongside hashes, separate content from commitment, and ground trust in verifiable chains of services; this thwarts circular self‑justification and enables robust cross‑chain entity derivation with PROV‑O.<cite id="fd82574d-4">Use PROV‑O’s derivation/attribution and qualified provenance to make semantics explicit and extensible</cite><cite id="4a7ee33b-4">Anchor compact proofs on‑chain and verify by recomputing hashes and checking contract‑bound proofs</cite><cite id="4a7ee33b-1">Carry and verify chains of service hashes to trace custody and transformations back to anchors</cite>.

Title: MultiChain Blockchain Data Provenance for Deterministic Stream Processing with Kafka Streams: A Weather Data Case Study
Snippet: In this work, we have used cryptographic tools such as hashing and Merkle root with the help of MultiChain blockchain to verify end-to-end provenance of a stream processing result. Predominantly concerning data provenance Merkle root and hash chains the are the mostly two used techniques. The two guarantee integrity, and don't explain any meaning. If they both purely used in the context of a simple stream processing pipeline, they verify end-to-end provenance, meaning tracing a result directly to the input of that result. In the case of complex streaming pipelines (e.g. window-joins), we need granularity of provenance steps to observe how step by step a result is concluded. In that case, Merkle root alone does not achieve the goal. Therefore, to achieve that goal a semantic layer should be added with this process, such as RDF [rdf()]. Moreover since verification cost of hash chains is linear, it will be not a proper solution for large number of records within a window. Although it is a satisfiable solution for less number of records. Therefore, Merkle root with logarithmic verification cost is an optimal solution.

Title: Verification Cost Asymmetry in Cognitive Warfare: A Complexity-Theoretic Framework
Snippet: Assumption 1 (Cryptographic Hardness). Collision-resistant hash functions exist, digital signatures satisfy existential unforgeability under chosen-message attack, and randomness beacons provide unpredictable sampling seeds. 

Theorem 1 (Constant-Work Verification). Under Assumption 1, there exists a protocol Π such that honest bundles produced by BuildBundle can be verified by population H in expected O(1) human steps for fixed parameter k, with soundness error δ(k) ≤ 2 −k . Proof Sketch. The construction combines Merkle tree commitments with redundancy-encoded provenance graphs. Each query location in Q corresponds to a consistency check between claimed sources and derived conclusions. By the PCP theorem, polynomial-size proofs can be verified with O(1) queries. Cryptographic binding via hash functions prevents adversaries from equivocating about the committed provenance structure. The exponential soundness bound follows from union bounds over independent spot-checks. 

For adversarial populations lacking access to precomputed bundles, verification costs scale with the complexity of the underlying provenance graph: Proposition 1 (Adversarial Lower Bound). Consider a model where adversary population A lacks access to committed provenance and operates under censorship hiding a Θ(n) fraction of sources. Any verification strategy that distinguishes honest from adversarial claims with advantage ϵ > 0 requires Ω(n 2 ) expected cross-source comparisons. 

Proof Sketch. We construct a family of claim distributions where ground truth depends on correlations between hidden sources. By Yao's minimax principle, any randomized verification algorithm must perform work equal to the worst-case deterministic cost. We show this worst case re-quires checking Ω(n 2 ) source pairs to detect planted inconsistencies with sufficient confidence, using information-theoretic arguments about distinguishing nearly-indistinguishable distributions.

Title: Cryptographically Assured Information Flow: Assured Remote Execution
Snippet: We keep track of "chains of provenance" for trust, meaning the sequence of services-starting from an anchor service-that obtained previous keys and generated new keys to protect for their successors. We store trust chains with the keys that they validate in protfor records. We also deliver trust chains in messages between parties, who can check them to trace provenance back to the anchoring program. 

Trust chains are lists of service hashes. If trch is a trust chain, we write the effect of pushing a new hash h to it as h :: trch, using a cons "::" operation. 

Each of the services we specify, when retrieving a trust chain, tests that its code hash is the first and the source service's hash is second. Thus, it has confirmed by the successful retrvfm that the prior entry also represented its identity correctly. When extending a trust chain, it pushes its intended recipient's hash to the front of the list. 

If an observer, seeing the trust chain, knows that the front n entries are compliant roles we have specified, it follows that the n + 1st entry is the actual source of the record retrieved by the nth entry. If that hash is also known to be compliant, this process can repeat. 

We have successfully designed and verified protocols relying on trust chains of length up to five (see § 9).

Title: Supporting Better Insights of Data Science Pipelines with Fine-grained Provenance
Snippet: In order to capture the provenance of a pipeline p of a combination of pre-processing operations o 1 , . . . , o n forming a tree, we introduce an abstract provenance-generating function (prov-gen), and associate it with each operation o k occurring in p. 

In accordance with the provenance model presented in Section 2.3, each element d ij of a dataset D produced during the execution of p is represented by a PROV entity in the provenance document. The properties of this entity include the row index i and feature j in D, and an identifier k denoting the fact that d ij is in the result of the operation o k in p. 

Similarly, each operation o k in p is represented by a PROV activity in the provenance document, whose properties specify the operator(s) illustrated in Section 2.2 that implement(s) o k , and the list of the features on which o k operates.

Snippet: Section 3 shows that distance-to-anchor hashing is reliable only when a view contains anchors that are locally relevant, and we need many such views to statistically form the localized hash via voting. We alleviate the high demand of anchors by an iterative bootstrapping framework that starts from a tiny seed set of paired anchors and grows it using multi-view hash collisions with posterior-guided promotion. 

Starting with L 0 := S, GEH generates L T through iterations. At iteration t, it derives L t by using inferred links identified at iteration t−1 in L t−1 as hash anchors, in three steps: 

is a subset of paired anchors of fixed size s t . 

• (Per-view link proposals) For each view A t,k , it computes view-specific distance-to-anchor hashes and proposes a set of candidate links P t,k ⊆ E 1 ×E 2 by nearestneighbor matching in the hash space. 

• (Posterior-guided bootstrapping) It aggregates all proposals into a confidence score for each candidate link and promotes high-confidence links as new anchors in L t . 

We next instantiate these three steps in full. 

View generation. At iteration t, we draw m t views, A t,1 , . . . , A t,mt ⊆ L t−1 , each of size s t . To stabilize early iterations, we include the seed set S in every view. This ensures views share a reliable core signal even when L t−1 is small. 

View sampling. The quality of a view depends on anchor diversity: clustered anchors yield redundant hash coordinates and poor stability. Hence, we choose each view by greedy Furthest Point Sampling (FPS) (Gonzalez, 1985) on one side of the paired anchors. Let B t−1 := L t−1 \ S, i.e., anchors bootstrapped at previous iteration t − 1. To form view A t,k , FPS starts from a random element of B t−1 and then iteratively adds the paired anchor whose (chosen-side) vector maximizes its minimum distance to the current subset. This encourages views with widely separated anchors and improves stability (see Appendix B.1 for detailed analysis). 

View scheduling. As bootstrapping (iteration) progresses, the anchor pool L t−1 grows.

Title: BlockA2A: Towards Secure and Verifiable Agent-to-Agent Interoperability
Snippet: The Data Anchoring Protocol (Protocol 8) extends the decentralized provenance framework established by the Task Initiation and State Transition Validation Protocols, providing the infrastructure to ensure long-term integrity for large data payloads (e.g., contracts, audit logs). In particular, the protocol addresses scalability by storing payloads off-chain in IPFS while anchoring their integrity on the blockchain. The workflow begins with the data owner hashing the payload (P ) using SHA-256 to generate H P , mirroring the hash computation in task initiation. The payload is then stored on IPFS, yielding a content identifier (CID P ) that uniquely maps to P 's content. Both H P , CID P , and a timestamp (t) are recorded on the Provenance Smart Contract-reusing the same contract infrastructure as prior protocols-to create an immutable link between the off-chain data and its on-chain proof. This allows third parties to verify P 's unaltered state at any time by recomputing H P and checking its existence in the contract, aligning with the multi-signature verification logic in Protocol 7. By separating storage (IPFS) from consensus (blockchain), the protocol efficiently manages large data while leveraging cryptographic guarantees. This design integrates seamlessly with task lifecycles: for example, a milestone in Protocol 7 might reference an anchored dataset, ensuring all stakeholders act on verifiably consistent information.

We alleviate the high demand of anchors by an iterative bootstrapping framework that starts from a tiny seed set of paired anchors and grows it using multi-view hash collisions with posterior-guided promotion. 

Starting with L 0 := S, GEH generates L T through iterations. At iteration t, it derives L t by using inferred links identified at iteration t−1 in L t−1 as hash anchors, in three steps: 

is a subset of paired anchors of fixed size s t . 

• (Per-view link proposals) For each view A t,k , it computes view-specific distance-to-anchor hashes and proposes a set of candidate links P t,k ⊆ E 1 ×E 2 by nearestneighbor matching in the hash space. 

• (Posterior-guided bootstrapping) It aggregates all proposals into a confidence score for each candidate link and promotes high-confidence links as new anchors in L t . 

We next instantiate these three steps in full. 

View generation. At iteration t, we draw m t views, A t,1 , . . . , A t,mt ⊆ L t−1 , each of size s t . To stabilize early iterations, we include the seed set S in every view. This ensures views share a reliable core signal even when L t−1 is small. 

View sampling. The quality of a view depends on anchor diversity: clustered anchors yield redundant hash coordinates and poor stability. Hence, we choose each view by greedy Furthest Point Sampling (FPS) (Gonzalez, 1985) on one side of the paired anchors. Let B t−1 := L t−1 \ S, i.e., anchors bootstrapped at previous iteration t − 1. To form view A t,k , FPS starts from a random element of B t−1 and then iteratively adds the paired anchor whose (chosen-side) vector maximizes its minimum distance to the current subset. This encourages views with widely separated anchors and improves stability (see Appendix B.1 for detailed analysis). 

View scheduling. As bootstrapping (iteration) progresses, the anchor pool L t−1 grows.

snippet.text:
We keep track of "chains of provenance" for trust, meaning the sequence of services-starting from an anchor service-that obtained previous keys and generated new keys to protect for their successors. We store trust chains with the keys that they validate in protfor records. We also deliver trust chains in messages between parties, who can check them to trace provenance back to the anchoring program. 

Trust chains are lists of service hashes. If trch is a trust chain, we write the effect of pushing a new hash h to it as h :: trch, using a cons "::" operation. 

Each of the services we specify, when retrieving a trust chain, tests that its code hash is the first and the source service's hash is second. Thus, it has confirmed by the successful retrvfm that the prior entry also represented its identity correctly. When extending a trust chain, it pushes its intended recipient's hash to the front of the list. 

If an observer, seeing the trust chain, knows that the front n entries are compliant roles we have specified, it follows that the n + 1st entry is the actual source of the record retrieved by the nth entry. If that hash is also known to be compliant, this process can repeat. 

We have successfully designed and verified protocols relying on trust chains of length up to five (see § 9).

snippet.text: The Data Anchoring Protocol (Protocol 8) extends the decentralized provenance framework established by the Task Initiation and State Transition Validation Protocols, providing the infrastructure to ensure long-term integrity for large data payloads (e.g., contracts, audit logs). In particular, the protocol addresses scalability by storing payloads off-chain in IPFS while anchoring their integrity on the blockchain. The workflow begins with the data owner hashing the payload (P ) using SHA-256 to generate H P , mirroring the hash computation in task initiation. The payload is then stored on IPFS, yielding a content identifier (CID P ) that uniquely maps to P 's content. Both H P , CID P , and a timestamp (t) are recorded on the Provenance Smart Contract-reusing the same contract infrastructure as prior protocols-to create an immutable link between the off-chain data and its on-chain proof. This allows third parties to verify P 's unaltered state at any time by recomputing H P and checking its existence in the contract, aligning with the multi-signature verification logic in Protocol 7. By separating storage (IPFS) from consensus (blockchain), the protocol efficiently manages large data while leveraging cryptographic guarantees. This design integrates seamlessly with task lifecycles: for example, a milestone in Protocol 7 might reference an anchored dataset, ensuring all stakeholders act on verifiably consistent information.

Title: Knowledge Graph Re-engineering Along the Ontological Continuum (extended version)
Snippet: Europeana uses the Europeana Data Model (EDM), capturing provenance through OAI-ORE Aggregations that record the original data provider, intermediaries, and Europeana as aggregator, with Dublin Core metadata at the core [26]. 

Google Data Commons extends Schema.org to attach a provenance property to every triple, recording the originating provider's URL as a first-class element of the data model [20,23]. 

Bio2RDF stores per-dataset provenance in dedicated named graphs, using VoID, PROV, and Dublin Core to describe conversion dates, licensing, and generating scripts [6]. 

The British Museum ResearchSpace platform uses RDF reification grounded in CIDOC-CRM to capture the provenance of scholarly assertions about cultural heritage objects [48]. 

UniProt has adopted RDF-Star to attach evidence and provenance annotations to individual triples, replacing a verbose and costly reification-based approach [25,49]. 

Wikidata provides fine-grained triple-level provenance through a bespoke statement model of qualifiers and references [51,28]. 

The EU Open Data Portal captures dataset provenance through DCAT-AP, incorporating PROV-O via prov:qualifiedAttribution to express agent roles and data lineage [31,14]. 

DBpedia organises Wikipedia-extracted data into named graphs per language and dataset, using PROV-O to record extraction process and originating source [2]. 

Linked Open Vocabularies (LOV) tracks vocabulary publication provenance using PROV-O, recording authors, publishers, versioning history, and curation agents [50]. 

Nanopublications treat provenance as a structural concern: each nanopublication comprises three named graphs: assertion, provenance, and publication info, with PROV-O capturing authorship, temporal data, and the epistemic status of scientific claims [21]. 

The ten KGs span the continuum along all four dimensions (see Table 1). The feature vocabulary is derived empirically during the analysis, reusing terms across KGs for consistency, not from a pre-existing controlled vocabulary.

Title: Enabling precision medicine via standard communication of HTS provenance, analysis, and results
Snippet: established to reliably communicate genomic data between databases and individual scientists.

An active community has engaged in provenance standardization to achieve these aims [28], culminating in the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) provenance specification (PROV) [29]. PROV Ontology (PROV-O) is used by FHIR and ROs and is based on the concept of generating an entity target via an agent's activity (see Fig 2). Workflow management systems capture analytic processes, while bioinformatic platforms capture analysis details. In combination, they provide a record of data provenance. Few, if any, systems and platforms offer a consistent method to accurately capture all facets of the various roles assumed by an agent who manipulates digital artifacts. BCO encourages adoption of standards such as PROV-O (https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-o/) and Open Researcher and Contributor ID (ORCID; https://orcid.org/) by defining how to recreate a complete history of what was computed, how it was computed, by whom it was computed, and why it was computed. Also known as the provenance domain, this section of BCOs incorporate the Provenance, Authoring and Versioning ontology (PAV, namespace http://purl.org/pav/) to capture "just enough" information to track how data are authored, curated, retrieved, and processed among many specific designations of an "agent."
