An active community has engaged in provenance standardization to achieve these aims [28], culminating in the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) provenance specification (PROV) [29]. PROV Ontology (PROV-O) is used by FHIR and ROs and is based on the concept of generating an entity target via an agent's activity (see Fig 2). Workflow management systems capture analytic processes, while bioinformatic platforms capture analysis details. In combination, they provide a record of data provenance. Few, if any, systems and platforms offer a consistent method to accurately capture all facets of the various roles assumed by an agent who manipulates digital artifacts. BCO encourages adoption of standards such as PROV-O (https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-o/) and Open Researcher and Contributor ID (ORCID; https://orcid.org/) by defining how to recreate a complete history of what was computed, how it was computed, by whom it was computed, and why it was computed. Also known as the provenance domain, this section of BCOs incorporate the Provenance, Authoring and Versioning ontology (PAV, namespace http://purl.org/pav/) to capture "just enough" information to track how data are authored, curated, retrieved, and processed among many specific designations of an "agent."

Snippet: The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

Title: QCIVET: A Quantum-Classical Pipeline Integrity Framework with Contract-Based Subtype Verification and Hash-Chained Audit Traces
Snippet: The state of the art for classical pipelines is built around attested provenance. in-toto [47] formalises a "farm-to-table" chain of attestations linking sources to artefacts; SLSA [43] layers a maturity model on top, with active analysis of adoption challenges [44]; Sigstore [33] offers keyless signing and a public transparency log. Recent work [35] systematises provenance, tamper resistance, and build integrity practices across this ecosystem. Closely related, hash-chain-based integrity verification has been used in adjacent domains [18,23,40], notably blockchain transaction auditing, and QCIVET inherits the chain-of-commitments idea from this line. 

These tools assume that the artefact under attestation is a binary, image, or package whose integrity is fully captured by a cryptographic hash of its bytes. This assumption holds for classical software but breaks for the quantum stages of a hybrid pipeline in two distinct ways. First, hardware noise: the same quantum circuit, when executed on a real QPU, can produce different outputs depending on the calibration drift and the prevailing single-and two-qubit error rates. Second, semantic substitution: a byte-level-conformant "sneaky" circuit (formally characterised in Section 5) may pass a weak observable contract while violating an informationally complete one. Two artefacts with identical hashes can therefore exhibit very different quantum behaviours. QCIVET inherits the hash-chain and external-anchor pattern from this literature (Sigstore Rekor and RFC 3161 [1] timestamping authorities are concrete instantiations of our ExternalAnchor interface) and extends it with an observable-deviation check at each quantum stage. Table 1 contrasts these classical supply-chain tools with QCIVET on three dimensions: hash-chain integrity, external anchoring, and quantum-stage scope. 

Table 1: Classical supply-chain integrity versus QCIVET.

Title: Verification Cost Asymmetry in Cognitive Warfare: A Complexity-Theoretic Framework
Snippet: Assumption 1 (Cryptographic Hardness). Collision-resistant hash functions exist, digital signatures satisfy existential unforgeability under chosen-message attack, and randomness beacons provide unpredictable sampling seeds. 

Theorem 1 (Constant-Work Verification). Under Assumption 1, there exists a protocol Π such that honest bundles produced by BuildBundle can be verified by population H in expected O(1) human steps for fixed parameter k, with soundness error δ(k) ≤ 2 −k . Proof Sketch. The construction combines Merkle tree commitments with redundancy-encoded provenance graphs. Each query location in Q corresponds to a consistency check between claimed sources and derived conclusions. By the PCP theorem, polynomial-size proofs can be verified with O(1) queries. Cryptographic binding via hash functions prevents adversaries from equivocating about the committed provenance structure. The exponential soundness bound follows from union bounds over independent spot-checks. 

For adversarial populations lacking access to precomputed bundles, verification costs scale with the complexity of the underlying provenance graph: Proposition 1 (Adversarial Lower Bound). Consider a model where adversary population A lacks access to committed provenance and operates under censorship hiding a Θ(n) fraction of sources. Any verification strategy that distinguishes honest from adversarial claims with advantage ϵ > 0 requires Ω(n 2 ) expected cross-source comparisons. 

Proof Sketch. We construct a family of claim distributions where ground truth depends on correlations between hidden sources. By Yao's minimax principle, any randomized verification algorithm must perform work equal to the worst-case deterministic cost. We show this worst case re-quires checking Ω(n 2 ) source pairs to detect planted inconsistencies with sufficient confidence, using information-theoretic arguments about distinguishing nearly-indistinguishable distributions.

Title: Cryptographically Assured Information Flow: Assured Remote Execution
Snippet: We keep track of "chains of provenance" for trust, meaning the sequence of services-starting from an anchor service-that obtained previous keys and generated new keys to protect for their successors. We store trust chains with the keys that they validate in protfor records. We also deliver trust chains in messages between parties, who can check them to trace provenance back to the anchoring program. 

Trust chains are lists of service hashes. If trch is a trust chain, we write the effect of pushing a new hash h to it as h :: trch, using a cons "::" operation. 

Each of the services we specify, when retrieving a trust chain, tests that its code hash is the first and the source service's hash is second. Thus, it has confirmed by the successful retrvfm that the prior entry also represented its identity correctly. When extending a trust chain, it pushes its intended recipient's hash to the front of the list. 

If an observer, seeing the trust chain, knows that the front n entries are compliant roles we have specified, it follows that the n + 1st entry is the actual source of the record retrieved by the nth entry. If that hash is also known to be compliant, this process can repeat. 

We have successfully designed and verified protocols relying on trust chains of length up to five (see § 9).

Title: Immutability Does Not Guarantee Trust: A Formal and Logical Refutation
Snippet: To rigorously dismantle the belief that immutability guarantees trust, we now construct formal counterexamples demonstrating their non-equivalence. These counterexamples do not merely refute the claim empirically; they expose its logical invalidity by constructing admissible models where immutability holds but rational trust does not follow. Each example is designed to isolate one of the flawed inferential steps commonly found in popular blockchain discourse. By formalising the conditions under which trust predicates fail to arise despite perfect immutability, we expose the category mistake that underlies this belief. The epistemic assumptions ascribed to structural properties are ungrounded. Immutability, as defined by hash-linked data integrity, is a mechanical constraint on alteration-not a guarantee of semantic content, ethical provenance, predictive validity, or system benevolence. 

What follows are illustrative constructions: a predictive fraud mechanism exploiting deterministic inclusion, and a pathological data inclusion scenario we term "garbage permanence." These cases instantiate models where Immutable(B) holds under cryptographic rigor, yet Trust A (B) is either irrational or unsound by predicate logic. This reveals a critical fissure between system design properties and user belief rationality-a fissure that must be explicitly acknowledged and never papered over by rhetorical analogy.

Title: Supporting Better Insights of Data Science Pipelines with Fine-grained Provenance
Snippet: In order to capture the provenance of a pipeline p of a combination of pre-processing operations o 1 , . . . , o n forming a tree, we introduce an abstract provenance-generating function (prov-gen), and associate it with each operation o k occurring in p. 

In accordance with the provenance model presented in Section 2.3, each element d ij of a dataset D produced during the execution of p is represented by a PROV entity in the provenance document. The properties of this entity include the row index i and feature j in D, and an identifier k denoting the fact that d ij is in the result of the operation o k in p. 

Similarly, each operation o k in p is represented by a PROV activity in the provenance document, whose properties specify the operator(s) illustrated in Section 2.2 that implement(s) o k , and the list of the features on which o k operates.

Following the PROV-O model, the provenance of an entity is either an entity (dataset, database, document, etc.) or an activity such as an external process (surveying, standards, estimation) or a computational process (value aggregation, inference rules for missing values, etc.). For geometries, provenance information propagates down the hierarchy. Title: PAV ontology: provenance, authoring and versioning
Snippet: Because Green's guideline has not been approved yet, we cannot state that his document replaces (dct:replaces) Doe's document. Also, Green's document is in the same form  and does not introduce substantive changes (dct: isVersionOf ) from Doe's document. PROV-O [3], an OWL ontology developed by the W3C Provenance Working group [13] aims to provide a standard for representing and exchanging domainindependent provenance information between applications and systems. PROV-O provides terms that can be used to trace the origin of a given resource, its derivation history, as well as the relationship between the resources, and the entities that contributed to the existence of the resource. PROV-O can be used at detailed process level with activity-agent-entity interactions, or at a higher level with shortcuts for entity-entity and entity-agent relations such as prov:wasDerivedFrom and prov:wasAttributedTo. 

Overall PROV-O is a generic provenance data model, which can be extended to give domain-specific provenance, for instance by subclasses of prov:Activity or subproperties of prov:wasAttributedTo. PROV-O does not itself provide any distinctions between authors, curators, contributors or artifact creators. 

PROV-O specifies a set of common extensions, which at first glance would seem to cover some of our requirements: i) prov:hadPrimarySource: a kind of "derivation relation from secondary materials to their primary sources, which were produced by some agent with direct experience and knowledge about the topic", ii) prov:was-QuotedFrom, the "repeat of (some or all of ) an entity, such as text or image, by someone who may or may not be its original author". 

However, on closer examination these terms are inadequate. For example, in the AlzSWAN project, curators consulted papers on the web.

attempts.answer:
Below we explain how smart-contract execution that depends on PROV-O provenance can violate blockchain consensus finality when the provenance is legitimately incomplete at transaction time, and we ground each step in evidence.

1) Setting: provenance and smart contracts
- Architectures exist to integrate PROV-compliant provenance with blockchains, where smart contracts publish or retrieve PROV data and enforce provenance-based constraints for auditing, access control, and traceability, with application developers deciding the granularity and purpose of recorded provenance<cite id="3f93480a-0">Architectures integrate PROV-compliant provenance with smart contracts for publishing/retrieving provenance; developers decide provenance granularity and purpose such as auditing, reliability, or access control</cite><cite id="3f93480a-1">Ontologies for supply chain provenance have been translated to Solidity to generate traces; RFID sensor data are captured and recorded to enable multi-party tracing</cite><cite id="3f93480a-3">Traceability ontologies can be applied in smart contracts to enforce traceability constraints and execute provenance traces in Ethereum</cite>. 
- In practice, provenance can be stored either on-chain or off-chain with contract-mediated validation; systems emphasize unforgeability, integrity, and auditability of provenance records, motivating coupling validation logic to provenance facts<cite id="3f93480a-0">A publish-provenance smart contract records provenance blocks following W3C PROV; retrieval smart contracts expose provenance to applications</cite><cite id="3f93480a-2">SmartProvenance uses Ethereum contracts to monitor operations and validate provenance change events via voting; unforgeability and tamper evidence are required</cite><cite id="3f93480a-2">Trusted hardware has been explored to ensure trustworthy generation and integrity/availability of provenance data</cite>.

2) PROV-O semantics and the problem of legitimate incompleteness
- PROV-O is an OWL ontology mapping PROV-DM’s entities, activities, and agents into RDF, enabling rich, interoperable provenance metadata; PROV is designed primarily for retrospective provenance, i.e., a-posteriori logs of steps that generated data resources<cite id="cbb6ff9b-0">PROV-O maps PROV-DM’s core constructs (entity, activity, agent) to RDF for interoperable provenance</cite><cite id="cbb6ff9b-1">PROV defines Entity, Activity, Agent with relations like used, wasAssociatedWith, wasGeneratedBy, wasDerivedFrom, wasAttributedTo; qualified terms add attributes (e.g., plan) and PROV is designed for retrospective provenance</cite><cite id="cbb6ff9b-2">PROV-O, along with PROV-DM and constraints, provides the canonical ontology-based representation of provenance; expanded terms capture activity details</cite><cite id="cbb6ff9b-3">The PROV family includes PROV-DM (data model), PROV-O (OWL ontology), and constraints for interoperable provenance representations</cite>. 
- Because provenance captures a history and is often retrospective, provenance graphs are inherently time-ordered, stepwise completed, and may include missing steps or evolving evidence at any moment; PROV’s retrospective focus implies that complete, stable evidence may only be available ex post, not at commit time<cite id="cbb6ff9b-1">W3C PROV is designed to describe retrospective provenance as a-posteriori logs of all steps executed to generate data</cite><cite id="cbb6ff9b-0">Provenance is used to assess quality and trustworthiness of data, grounded in entities, activities, and agents involved</cite>. 
- In smart-contract settings, applications and contracts decide the granularity of provenance captured (on IoT/supply-chain workflows), which creates a practical gap between what is needed to decide execution and what is available when a transaction is submitted and needs immediate validation<cite id="3f93480a-0">Developers choose the level of granularity and purpose (audit, reliability, access control) for provenance maintained on-chain</cite><cite id="3f93480a-1">Supply-chain provenance traces are generated by sensor-triggered records and contracts to support multi-party auditing</cite>.

3) What consensus/finality requires from smart contract execution
- For consensus to be final, execution must guarantee integrity/atomicity (exactly-once state transition), liveness/progress (transactions eventually complete under conditions), and determinism: given the same system state and inputs, validators compute the same next state and reach agreement; off-chain or externally visible side effects must be bounded so that agreement implies durable, irreversible outcome<cite id="3f93480a-3">Smart contracts can enforce traceability constraints and execute provenance traces; such constraints are part of the on-chain logic that must remain consistent</cite><cite id="3f93480a-2">Contract-mediated validation of provenance changes and voting mechanisms imply deterministic acceptance rules for on-chain records</cite>. 
- When execution logic is expressed in ontologies and governance structures embedded at the protocol level (e.g., DAO), correctness hinges on well-defined semantic mappings and termination semantics for governance workflows; violations can cascade to protocol-level reorganizations if validation predicates change meaning or complete incompletely<cite id="d0d1f706-3">Encoding governance ontologies at the protocol level via ontology-to-smart-contract encoding is proposed; analysis of The DAO illustrates how governance semantics affect protocol behavior</cite><cite id="d0d1f706-4">Ontologies for smart-contract languages (Solidity) are proposed to improve data validation and contract generation with reusable knowledge</cite>.

4) How legitimate provenance incompleteness at commit time undermines finality

4.1 Unstable validation predicates break determinism and uniqueness
- If a contract’s accept clause depends on PROV-O assertions (e.g., “this transfer was authorized by a vetted provenance step”), and those assertions are not yet present or are being appended asynchronously, then the same transaction may yield different outcomes across validators at different times, violating deterministic agreement and leading to split acceptance or repeated re-submission<cite id="3f93480a-0">Provenance publication and retrieval are mediated by smart contracts; the developer controls granularity, which can mean some facts are not yet available at commit time</cite><cite id="3f93480a-1">Sensor-driven provenance is captured and recorded; availability and ordering are tied to device events and blockchain recording</cite><cite id="cbb6ff9b-1">PROV is retrospective: provenance describes steps that occurred, so evidence unfolds over time and may not be complete at any instant</cite>. 
- This manifests as transactional nondeterminism: validators either (a) have not seen the latest prov:wasGeneratedBy/prov:wasAssociatedWith edges by block N, or (b) received them via asynchronous channels; thus, block N accepts/ rejects the transaction inconsistently, creating forks without a common future and eroding finality<cite id="cbb6ff9b-1">Key PROV relations include wasGeneratedBy, wasAssociatedWith, wasAttributedTo, and qualified patterns to describe activity details; these relations define the causal edges a provenance graph must have</cite><cite id="3f93480a-0">Provenance publication and retrieval are contract-triggered operations whose timing and completeness are under developer control and network latency</cite>. 
- Even “final” blocks can later adopt stricter provenance filters (e.g., additional qualified constraints or expanded agents), causing rollbacks to retroactively invalidate prior execution outcomes, undermining the immutability of effects and user expectations of closure<cite id="d0d1f706-3">Protocol-level governance ontologies can be embedded; changes to governance semantics can propagate to validated workflows, affecting their termination and acceptance</cite><cite id="3f93480a-2">Contract-mediated validation of provenance changes can be governed by voting protocols that alter acceptance predicates over time</cite>.

4.2 Externally sourced evidence (oracle/provenance) destroys integrity and liveness guarantees
- Many provenance-backed contracts rely on external data (e.g., sensor records, identity attestations) that are asynchronously written to the blockchain or off-chain; if those facts are not yet visible to validators at transaction time, execution branches on uncertain predicates, creating ambiguity and potential conflicts across validators and chains<cite id="3f93480a-1">Sensor data adjust to smart contracts and are recorded on the blockchain; provenance traces become accessible for tracing</cite><cite id="3f93480a-0">Applications publish or query provenance data via REST/contracts; the timing and completeness are determined by the application-defined granularity and network delays</cite>. 
- Because PROV-O is retrospective, validators may later observe new prov:used or prov:wasInformedBy edges that change the trustworthiness assessment of earlier data, which can retroactively flip acceptance/rejection decisions and trigger reorgs or compensatory transactions, violating integrity (irreversibility) and liveness (users retry indefinitely under uncertainty)<cite id="cbb6ff9b-1">PROV is a-posteriori: provenance traces are logs of steps taken, so additional steps and attributes may be discovered after-the-fact</cite><cite id="3f93480a-2">Voting-based provenance validation and unforgeability constraints create mechanisms that can alter accepted provenance histories over time</cite>. 
- In supply-chain/DeFi settings, this mirrors oracle attacks and oracle-lag scenarios: if contract execution hinges on “evidence is available and unaltered,” then delayed or missing provenance receipts can be exploited by adversaries or cause cascading invalidations; the chain’s fork-agnostic acceptance predicates then fail to converge, eroding finality<cite id="d0d1f706-0">A behavioristic semantic approach discusses conjoining blockchain with ontologies for services and resources, highlighting that semantic descriptions remain poor for smart-contract outcomes, impeding deterministic discovery</cite><cite id="3f93480a-1">Ontology-based provenance traces for physical goods enable auditability and fraud-fighting; reliance on recorded, external sensor data underlines the need for timely, complete evidence</cite>.

4.3 Invalidation cascades and protocol-level governance failures
- When governance semantics are encoded in ontologies and contracts (e.g., “only entities with vetted provenance can finalize”), changing or incompletely codified provenance graphs can alter the acceptability of prior blocks or transactions; protocol-level analyses of The DAO show how governance predicates, if semantically underspecified or changeable, can produce non-terminating workflows and reorganizations under stress conditions<cite id="d0d1f706-3">Encoding governance ontologies at protocol level and analyzing The DAO illustrate how governance semantics propagate to execution and can affect termination and acceptance</cite><cite id="d0d1f706-4">Ontologies for smart-contract languages emphasize data validation; underspecified semantics preclude discovery of outcomes, risking nondeterminism</cite>. 
- This directly violates finality: validators cannot agree on a unique next state if later provenance updates retroactively alter validation predicates; users cannot rely on “final” receipts because new evidence can overturn decisions, and chains may reorganize to reflect stricter provenance policies adopted ex post<cite id="3f93480a-2">Voting protocols for provenance changes imply that acceptance depends on ongoing governance processes, not just static facts</cite><cite id="cbb6ff9b-1">Qualified patterns and retrospective logging mean validation may depend on facts yet to be recorded in the provenance graph</cite>.

5) Concrete patterns and mitigations
- Keep provenance receipts on-chain and final-cement them with receipts: contracts validate against receipts that are append-only and visible at commit time, avoiding reliance on future provenance edges; this preserves deterministic acceptance and irreversible state change<cite id="3f93480a-0">Provenance can be stored in blocks under a Provenance Blockchain and retrieved via contracts to decide access and auditing</cite><cite id="3f93480a-2">Auditors validate using receipts; trusted generation and integrity/availability mechanisms reduce forgeability</cite>. 
- Use trusted generation to bound incompleteness: tie provenance creation to tamper-evident hardware or secure enclaves and encode constraints so that necessary edges exist before execution, limiting late-binding validation to read-only queries<cite id="3f93480a-2">Prov-Trust leverages SGX to provide trustworthy provenance data; unforgeability and tamper evidence are enforced to ensure integrity and availability</cite>. 
- Encode validation as monotone, conservative filters: accept only if all qualified provenance attributes are satisfied and remain satisfied under future graph completions; otherwise delay acceptance or use atomic cross-contract channels to ensure at-least-once, order-preserving validation before commit; this preserves uniqueness and liveness at the cost of latency and potential retries<cite id="cbb6ff9b-1">Qualified terms provide additional attributes to binary relations (e.g., plan) and PROV is retrospective, implying conservative acceptance requires accounting for future evidence</cite><cite id="3f93480a-0">Applications can choose granularity and timing of provenance publication, enabling staged validation that waits for necessary facts</cite>. 
- Formalize governance semantics at protocol level: define stable, versioned provenance ontologies and acceptance predicates in upgrade-protected modules; prohibit retroactive predicate flips that would invalidate prior transactions, aligning with consensus finality expectations<cite id="d0d1f706-3">Ontology of governance at protocol level, derived from analyzing The DAO, suggests encoding stable governance semantics to avoid non-terminating behavior</cite>.

6) Summary: violation pathways and alignment
- The core violations are: nondeterministic acceptance due to incomplete or evolving provenance graphs, integrity loss from retroactive evidence flips, and liveness loss from retries and reorgs when uncertainty persists; these arise because PROV-O is retrospective and contracts depend on facts that unfold asynchronously across validators and chains<cite id="cbb6ff9b-1">PROV is a-posteriori; provenance logs describe steps that happened, and qualified/expanded relations capture details that unfold over time</cite><cite id="3f93480a-0">Contract-triggered provenance publication/retrieval depends on developer-chosen granularity and network timing, creating legitimate incompleteness at transaction time</cite><cite id="3f93480a-2">Contract-mediated validation and voting mechanisms can change acceptance over time, enabling rollbacks or rejections of previously accepted outcomes</cite>. 
- Designs that align with finality enforce on-chain, tamper-evident provenance receipts visible to validators at commit; use conservative, monotone acceptance filters with explicit deadlines; and freeze semantics of acceptance predicates at protocol level so that “final” outcomes remain uniquely determinable and irreversible under known provenance semantics<cite id="3f93480a-2">On-chain receipts and trusted generation support unforgeability, enabling deterministic, tamper-evident validation</cite><cite id="cbb6ff9b-1">Qualified, retrospective PROV patterns require conservative acceptance to account for evidence completeness</cite><cite id="d0d1f706-3">Protocol-level governance ontologies aim to prevent non-terminating workflows by stabilizing semantics</cite>.

Title: Towards a Blockchain-based Architecture for Data Provenance Management in the Internet of Things
Snippet: This section describes the proposed architecture aiming to maintain provenance records, based on a blockchain infrastructure, and also provides two examples of its application. 

The concepts of an IoT architecture with data provenance support [Hu et al. 2020] are presented in Figure 1. The architecture we propose is located in the Middleware Layer and assumes that the other layers are defined and fully functioning. • Rest API: API designed to mediate the requests between the IoT Application and the smart contracts. It provides the IoT Application with operations to publish or to query the provenance data of a given object (thing) in the Provenance Blockchain. 

• Publish Provenance Smart Contract: smart contract triggered by the Rest API, responsible for publishing provenance data to the Provenance Blockchain. • Retrieve Provenance Smart Contract: smart contract triggered by Rest API, responsible for browsing the Provenance Blockchain for provenance data, based on the given search criteria, and returning it to the Rest API, which in turn forwards it to the IoT Application. • Provenance Blockchain: blockchain infrastructure where provenance data is stored in the form of blocks, following the W3C PROV standard. 

The proposed architecture aims to facilitate the management of provenance data for the IoT application developer. Therefore, the developer can simply perform calls to the Rest API in order to publish or retrieve provenance data about a given object (thing) that is stored in the Provenance Blockchain. It remains with the developer to decide the level of granularity of the provenance that will be maintained (i.e., which provenance data will be recorded and how often), as well as its purpose, which can be, for instance, to enable auditing over the application in case of failures or abnormal behavior, to ensure the reliability of the objects and their produced data, or to maintain access control over the information generated by the application.
</snippet>

Title: Prov-Trust: Towards a Trustworthy SGX-based Data Provenance System
Snippet: The provenance data are stored in transactions that are broadcasted to the core of blockchain network created by a specific set of validating virtual machines. Similar to Provchain solution, the provenance auditor validates the data using the transactions receipts. SmartProvenance (Ramachandran and Kantarcioglu, 2018) applies Ethereum Smart Contracts to provide data provenance. SmartProvenance is based on two smart contracts, namely Document Tracker contract and Vote contract. The Document Tracker smart contract is used to monitor the operations performed over a given document while the vote contract specifies the voting protocol. A voting process is used to validate every provenance change event. 

These solutions do not address a trusted generation of the provenance data, yet unforgeability is a security requirement that needs to be achieved while generating and storing provenance data. The unforgeability means that an adversary cannot forge a valid provenance record either by modifying any existing one or directly introducing a new forged provenance record without being detected. Hence, unforgeability guarantees the tamper evidence (Asghar et al., 2012;Taha et al., 2015). A first attempt to use Trusted Platform Module to ensure trust in provenance generation had been introduced by Bock et al. (Böck et al., 2010). This solution presented a data provenance collection solution using a TPM chip and the AMD Secure Virtual Machine (SVM) technology. This solution has been enhanced further by Taha et al. (Taha et al., 2015) by adding the integrity and availability of the provenance data to the solution. 

In our proposed solution Prov-Trust, we leverage Blockchain technology and trusted hardware; the Intel SGX to provide trustworthy and secure provenance data.
</snippet>

Title: A First Step in the Co-Evolution of Blockchain and Ontologies: Towards Engineering an Ontology of Governance at the Blockchain Protocol Level
Snippet: At the beginning of 2018, there is a growing belief that blockchain technologies constitute a revolutionary innovation in how we transfer value electronically. In that vein, blockchain may be a suitable complement to ontologies to truly achieve Tim Berners-Lee's vision of the semantic Web. We believe that if this complementarity is to be achieved blockchain and ontologies must co-evolve. In this paper, we focus on what and how to engineer artifacts (models, methods, designs, and implementations) for this co-evolution. 

Specifically, we posit that a pragmatic first step in co-evolving blockchain with ontologies is to encode ontology representations as meta-data tags to be embedded and instantiated in a smart contract at the blockchain protocol level. We further posit that an ontology representing governance structure is more likely to be adopted by smart contract writers than ontologies representing other domains. Finally, we analyze the smart contracts of the infamous The DAO experiment on Ethereum, from which we outline a conceptual design for a governance ontology at the blockchain protocol level. 

There is much more work to be done. As a start, the prototype design outlined in this paper must be implemented in Ethereum or another blockchain environment. Also, a more complete analysis of smart contract governance structures, including development of a more structured ontology remains to be done. This paper serves as an initial roadmap for engineering artifacts for blockchain/ontology co-evolution, and there are many design issues that need to be more fully explored. Title: Toward the Ontological Modeling of Smart Contracts: A Solidity Use Case
Snippet: One technique for representing knowledge is the use of ontologies, providing the ability to process semantics since ontologies encompass a representation, formal naming, and definition of categories, properties, and relations between concepts, data and entities that substantiate one, many or all domains of discourse. 

One domain of Knowledge Representation is programming languages, for which already exists ontologies that cover or model popular programming languages, such as Java and C. The use of Knowledge Representation applied to programming languages has improved current educational techniques and complemented some of these languages, providing additional parsers, code generators, or code validation. However, despite the popularity of smart contracts and the fact that they are also programs, and thus, expressed according to one programming language, there is no ontology oriented to represent smart contracts themselves. 

Smart contracts could benefit from the knowledge representation capabilities provided by ontologies in areas such as data validation, contract generation or extending the knowledge of a domain with other domains, inter alia. In this paper, an ontology for a smart contract language is presented, Solidity, which is the main smart contract language for one of the most relevant blockchain technologies, Ethereum [9], bringing knowledge representation for this language, linking the ontology to standard ontologies and making its knowledge reusable. Furthermore, this ontology has been evaluated with contracts already deployed in the Ethereum blockchain to assess its completeness. 

This work is organised as follows: Section II introduces the state of the art of smart contracts and ontologies. Then, Section III presents previous work done with ontologies and programming languages or smart contracts. Next, section IV details how the ontology was developed and explains the structure of the Solidity ontology. After that, Section V presents the evaluation method used and the results obtained. Finally, section VI recapitulates the conclusions obtained based on the results achieved and presents future lines of work.

Snippet: The PROV specification is a recognized standard in the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) dedicated for the provenance interchange on the web [57]. In PROV (Figure 5), the provenance comes from the information about entities, activities, and people involved in producing a piece of data or thing [58]. The provenance information is often used to form assessments about the quality, reliability, or trustworthiness of data. In the PROV family of models, PROV-DM is the conceptual data model that presents the core model that constitutes the foundation for the W3C Provenance (PROV) family of specifications [59]. PROV-O is the PROV Ontology, an OWL2 ontology allowing the mapping of the PROV data model to RDF [60]. Three main components, prov:entity, prov:activity, and prov:agent, express, respectively, the data flow view, the process flow, and the responsibility view.
</snippet>

Title: Data Provenance
Snippet: Although there exist several provenance models used in specific settings promoted by different international initiatives, the main basic standard widely-used and referred to is the W3C's PROV recommendation 2 , which evolved from the Open Provenance Model (OPM). After three international workshops [1] on provenance standardisation, OPM was developed in 2010 and subsequently adopted by many workflow systems. PROV is very much influenced by OPM and was released as a standard by the W3C Provenance Working Group in April 2013. The W3C PROV Recommendation [2] consists of some constituent standards including for PROV XML 3 and PROV as an ontology for RDFbased data (PROV-O) 4 . 

The essential elements (see Fig. 1) of the PROV ontology are called Starting Point Terms and consist of three primary classes with unique and mandatory identifiers and nine properties to describe the relations between the classes. The three classes are prov:Entity which is the central concept and represents resources, prov:Activity representing actions performed upon entities, and prov:Agent representing persons or machines who bears some form of responsibility for an activity. The most important relationships are: used (an activity used some artefact), wasAssociatedWith (an agent participated in some activity), wasGeneratedBy (an activity generated an entity), wasDerivedFrom (an entity was derived from another entity), wasAttributedTo (an entity was attributed to an agent), actedOnBehalfOf (an agent acted on behalf of another agent) and wasInformedBy (an activity used an entity produced by another activity). Expanded terms are used to specialise agents and entities and to introduce time validity descriptions for activities. Qualified terms are used to provide additional attributes of the binary relations introducing so-called qualified patterns. In this way it is possible to add for example the concept 'plan', an association class, to describe more in detail how an activity was carried out. W3C PROV has primarily been designed to describe retrospective provenance (rprov) which refers to a-posteriori descriptions of provenance traces of data resources, i.e. provenance as an extended log of all the steps executed to generate the data entity.
</snippet>

Title: Semantic Provenance Graph for Reproducibility of Biomedical Research Studies: Generating and Analyzing Graph Structures from Published Literature
Snippet: The W3C PROV specifications consists of: (1) the core model called PROV-DM, which defines a common terminology system for representing interoperable provenance metadata [19]; (b) the PROV Ontology (PROV-O) that represents PROV-DM in the W3C Web Ontology Language (OWL2) [12; 16]; and a set of constraints (PROV-Constraints) to define valid forms of provenance conforming to the PROV specifications [4]. We extended PROV-O in the ProvCaRe project to model provenance terms associated with biomedical research studies. In particular, we extended the three core concepts of PROV-O, namely "prov:Agent", "prov:Entity", "prov:Activity"; and its properties, namely "prov:wasDerivedFrom", "prov:wasGeneratedBy", and "prov:used". The namespace prov refers to "http://www.w3.org/ns/prov#". 

ProvCaRe Knowledge Repository: The provenance terms extracted by the ProvCaRe NLP pipeline is currently stored in the ProvCaRe knowledge repository as set of three related provenance terms (for a detailed description of the NLP pipeline, we refer to [23]). For example, we stored provenance terms extracted from an article describing study on sleepdisordered breathing and hypertension by O'Connor et al. [20] as "hypertension status of participants", "was ascertained at", "second follow-up exam" in the ProvCaRe knowledge repository. However, this representation of provenance metadata has some limitations, for example (1) it is verbose (making it difficult to query efficiently); and (2) it cannot be modeled as a RDF graph structure. Given a user query, "How was the hypertension status of participants determined in this research study?", the ProvCaRe query interface uses keyword-based matching together with ontology-based "expansion" of query expression for retrieving query results.

Snippet: The specifications define a data model and an OWL ontology, along with a number of serializations for representing aspects of provenance. The term provenance, as understood in these specifications, refers to information about entities, activities, and people involved in producing a piece of data or thing, which can be used to form assessments about its quality, reliability or trustworthiness (PROV-Overview [w3c12]). The specifications include a combination of W3C Recommendation and Note documents. Recommendation documents include (i) the main PROV data model specification (PROV-DM [MMB + 12]), with an associated set of constraints and inference rules (PROV-CONSTRAINTS [CMM12]); (ii) an OWL ontology that allows a mapping of the data model to RDF (PROV-O [LSM + 12]), and (iii) a notation for PROV with a relational-like syntax, aimed at human consumption (PROV-N [MMCSR12]). All other documents are Notes. These include PROV-XML, which defines a XSD schema for XML serialization [pro13c]. PROV-AQ, the Provenance Access and Query document [MHS + 12], which defines a Web-compliant mechanism to associate a dataset to its provenance; PROV-DICTIONARY [pro13b], for expressing the provenance of data collections defined as sets of key-entity pairs; and PROV-DC [pro13a], which provides a mapping between PROV-O and Dublin Core Terms.

Title: Data provenance, curation and quality in metrology
Snippet: Provenance information exists in many domain-specific standards 16,17 . There is also a World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) provenance interoperability standard called W3C PROV 18,19 . The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) is the main standards body for the World Wide Web, and has created many standards (called Recommendations) including HTML (used for web pages), RDF (a data model for descriptive information using subjectpredicate-object triples), and OWL, a language for defining ontologies for RDF data. In this context, "ontology" means a set of classes (defining kinds of things), properties (defining kinds of relationships between the things), and rules that impose constraints on the classes and properties, or define ways to infer new knowledge from existing facts. RDF and OWL are used to represent data in the Semantic Web / Linked Data settings, which have been proposed as ways to make data on the Web more machine-readable and more useful for automated analysis. 

The Provenance Interchange Working Group was active from 2011-2013 and produced several W3C Recommendations as well as a number of supporting W3C Notes (documents that support and explain standards, but do not themselves specify standard behaviour). The four main Recommendations are: 

• PROV-DM -which specifies the PROV Data Model, a collection of vocabulary terms used in the PROV standards and their intended meanings f • PROV-N -which specifies the PROV Notation (also called PROV-N), a serialization format for PROV information that is intended to be both human and machine readable g • PROV-O -which specifies a PROV Ontology (also called PROV-O), an OWL ontology that specifies basic constraints and usage for PROV Of these standards, PROV-DM and PROV-O are probably the most relevant for typical uses of provenance in the Semantic Web (that is, using RDF and OWL). Other formats for PROV based on XML and JSON have also been defined, but as supporting documents rather than formal Recommendations. The design rationale and lessons learned from the development of PROV are described by Moreau et al. 20 . Since PROV has now superseded earlier proposals, we do not go into further details about them.

Below we explain how smart-contract execution that depends on PROV-O provenance can violate blockchain consensus finality when the provenance is legitimately incomplete at transaction time, and we ground each step in evidence.

1) Setting: provenance and smart contracts
- Architectures exist to integrate PROV-compliant provenance with blockchains, where smart contracts publish or retrieve PROV data and enforce provenance-based constraints for auditing, access control, and traceability, with application developers deciding the granularity and purpose of recorded provenance<cite id="3f93480a-0">Architectures integrate PROV-compliant provenance with smart contracts for publishing/retrieving provenance; developers decide provenance granularity and purpose such as auditing, reliability, or access control</cite><cite id="3f93480a-1">Ontologies for supply chain provenance have been translated to Solidity to generate traces; RFID sensor data are captured and recorded to enable multi-party tracing</cite><cite id="3f93480a-3">Traceability ontologies can be applied in smart contracts to enforce traceability constraints and execute provenance traces in Ethereum</cite>. 
- In practice, provenance can be stored either on-chain or off-chain with contract-mediated validation; systems emphasize unforgeability, integrity, and auditability of provenance records, motivating coupling validation logic to provenance facts<cite id="3f93480a-0">A publish-provenance smart contract records provenance blocks following W3C PROV; retrieval smart contracts expose provenance to applications</cite><cite id="3f93480a-2">SmartProvenance uses Ethereum contracts to monitor operations and validate provenance change events via voting; unforgeability and tamper evidence are required</cite><cite id="3f93480a-2">Trusted hardware has been explored to ensure trustworthy generation and integrity/availability of provenance data</cite>.

2) PROV-O semantics and the problem of legitimate incompleteness
- PROV-O is an OWL ontology mapping PROV-DM’s entities, activities, and agents into RDF, enabling rich, interoperable provenance metadata; PROV is designed primarily for retrospective provenance, i.e., a-posteriori logs of steps that generated data resources<cite id="cbb6ff9b-0">PROV-O maps PROV-DM’s core constructs (entity, activity, agent) to RDF for interoperable provenance</cite><cite id="cbb6ff9b-1">PROV defines Entity, Activity, Agent with relations like used, wasAssociatedWith, wasGeneratedBy, wasDerivedFrom, wasAttributedTo; qualified terms add attributes (e.g., plan) and PROV is designed for retrospective provenance</cite><cite id="cbb6ff9b-2">PROV-O, along with PROV-DM and constraints, provides the canonical ontology-based representation of provenance; expanded terms capture activity details</cite><cite id="cbb6ff9b-3">The PROV family includes PROV-DM (data model), PROV-O (OWL ontology), and constraints for interoperable provenance representations</cite>. 
- Because provenance captures a history and is often retrospective, provenance graphs are inherently time-ordered, stepwise completed, and may include missing steps or evolving evidence at any moment; PROV’s retrospective focus implies that complete, stable evidence may only be available ex post, not at commit time<cite id="cbb6ff9b-1">W3C PROV is designed to describe retrospective provenance as a-posteriori logs of all steps executed to generate data</cite><cite id="cbb6ff9b-0">Provenance is used to assess quality and trustworthiness of data, grounded in entities, activities, and agents involved</cite>. 
- In smart-contract settings, applications and contracts decide the granularity of provenance captured (on IoT/supply-chain workflows), which creates a practical gap between what is needed to decide execution and what is available when a transaction is submitted and needs immediate validation<cite id="3f93480a-0">Developers choose the level of granularity and purpose (audit, reliability, access control) for provenance maintained on-chain</cite><cite id="3f93480a-1">Supply-chain provenance traces are generated by sensor-triggered records and contracts to support multi-party auditing</cite>.

3) What consensus/finality requires from smart contract execution
- For consensus to be final, execution must guarantee integrity/atomicity (exactly-once state transition), liveness/progress (transactions eventually complete under conditions), and determinism: given the same system state and inputs, validators compute the same next state and reach agreement; off-chain or externally visible side effects must be bounded so that agreement implies durable, irreversible outcome<cite id="3f93480a-3">Smart contracts can enforce traceability constraints and execute provenance traces; such constraints are part of the on-chain logic that must remain consistent</cite><cite id="3f93480a-2">Contract-mediated validation of provenance changes and voting mechanisms imply deterministic acceptance rules for on-chain records</cite>. 
- When execution logic is expressed in ontologies and governance structures embedded at the protocol level (e.g., DAO), correctness hinges on well-defined semantic mappings and termination semantics for governance workflows; violations can cascade to protocol-level reorganizations if validation predicates change meaning or complete incompletely<cite id="d0d1f706-3">Encoding governance ontologies at the protocol level via ontology-to-smart-contract encoding is proposed; analysis of The DAO illustrates how governance semantics affect protocol behavior</cite><cite id="d0d1f706-4">Ontologies for smart-contract languages (Solidity) are proposed to improve data validation and contract generation with reusable knowledge</cite>.

4) How legitimate provenance incompleteness at commit time undermines finality

4.1 Unstable validation predicates break determinism and uniqueness
- If a contract’s accept clause depends on PROV-O assertions (e.g., “this transfer was authorized by a vetted provenance step”), and those assertions are not yet present or are being appended asynchronously, then the same transaction may yield different outcomes across validators at different times, violating deterministic agreement and leading to split acceptance or repeated re-submission<cite id="3f93480a-0">Provenance publication and retrieval are mediated by smart contracts; the developer controls granularity, which can mean some facts are not yet available at commit time</cite><cite id="3f93480a-1">Sensor-driven provenance is captured and recorded; availability and ordering are tied to device events and blockchain recording</cite><cite id="cbb6ff9b-1">PROV is retrospective: provenance describes steps that occurred, so evidence unfolds over time and may not be complete at any instant</cite>. 
- This manifests as transactional nondeterminism: validators either (a) have not seen the latest prov:wasGeneratedBy/prov:wasAssociatedWith edges by block N, or (b) received them via asynchronous channels; thus, block N accepts/ rejects the transaction inconsistently, creating forks without a common future and eroding finality<cite id="cbb6ff9b-1">Key PROV relations include wasGeneratedBy, wasAssociatedWith, wasAttributedTo, and qualified patterns to describe activity details; these relations define the causal edges a provenance graph must have</cite><cite id="3f93480a-0">Provenance publication and retrieval are contract-triggered operations whose timing and completeness are under developer control and network latency</cite>. 
- Even “final” blocks can later adopt stricter provenance filters (e.g., additional qualified constraints or expanded agents), causing rollbacks to retroactively invalidate prior execution outcomes, undermining the immutability of effects and user expectations of closure<cite id="d0d1f706-3">Protocol-level governance ontologies can be embedded; changes to governance semantics can propagate to validated workflows, affecting their termination and acceptance</cite><cite id="3f93480a-2">Contract-mediated validation of provenance changes can be governed by voting protocols that alter acceptance predicates over time</cite>.

4.2 Externally sourced evidence (oracle/provenance) destroys integrity and liveness guarantees
- Many provenance-backed contracts rely on external data (e.g., sensor records, identity attestations) that are asynchronously written to the blockchain or off-chain; if those facts are not yet visible to validators at transaction time, execution branches on uncertain predicates, creating ambiguity and potential conflicts across validators and chains<cite id="3f93480a-1">Sensor data adjust to smart contracts and are recorded on the blockchain; provenance traces become accessible for tracing</cite><cite id="3f93480a-0">Applications publish or query provenance data via REST/contracts; the timing and completeness are determined by the application-defined granularity and network delays</cite>. 
- Because PROV-O is retrospective, validators may later observe new prov:used or prov:wasInformedBy edges that change the trustworthiness assessment of earlier data, which can retroactively flip acceptance/rejection decisions and trigger reorgs or compensatory transactions, violating integrity (irreversibility) and liveness (users retry indefinitely under uncertainty)<cite id="cbb6ff9b-1">PROV is a-posteriori: provenance traces are logs of steps taken, so additional steps and attributes may be discovered after-the-fact</cite><cite id="3f93480a-2">Voting-based provenance validation and unforgeability constraints create mechanisms that can alter accepted provenance histories over time</cite>. 
- In supply-chain/DeFi settings, this mirrors oracle attacks and oracle-lag scenarios: if contract execution hinges on “evidence is available and unaltered,” then delayed or missing provenance receipts can be exploited by adversaries or cause cascading invalidations; the chain’s fork-agnostic acceptance predicates then fail to converge, eroding finality<cite id="d0d1f706-0">A behavioristic semantic approach discusses conjoining blockchain with ontologies for services and resources, highlighting that semantic descriptions remain poor for smart-contract outcomes, impeding deterministic discovery</cite><cite id="3f93480a-1">Ontology-based provenance traces for physical goods enable auditability and fraud-fighting; reliance on recorded, external sensor data underlines the need for timely, complete evidence</cite>.

4.3 Invalidation cascades and protocol-level governance failures
- When governance semantics are encoded in ontologies and contracts (e.g., “only entities with vetted provenance can finalize”), changing or incompletely codified provenance graphs can alter the acceptability of prior blocks or transactions; protocol-level analyses of The DAO show how governance predicates, if semantically underspecified or changeable, can produce non-terminating workflows and reorganizations under stress conditions<cite id="d0d1f706-3">Encoding governance ontologies at protocol level and analyzing The DAO illustrate how governance semantics propagate to execution and can affect termination and acceptance</cite><cite id="d0d1f706-4">Ontologies for smart-contract languages emphasize data validation; underspecified semantics preclude discovery of outcomes, risking nondeterminism</cite>. 
- This directly violates finality: validators cannot agree on a unique next state if later provenance updates retroactively alter validation predicates; users cannot rely on “final” receipts because new evidence can overturn decisions, and chains may reorganize to reflect stricter provenance policies adopted ex post<cite id="3f93480a-2">Voting protocols for provenance changes imply that acceptance depends on ongoing governance processes, not just static facts</cite><cite id="cbb6ff9b-1">Qualified patterns and retrospective logging mean validation may depend on facts yet to be recorded in the provenance graph</cite>.

5) Concrete patterns and mitigations
- Keep provenance receipts on-chain and final-cement them with receipts: contracts validate against receipts that are append-only and visible at commit time, avoiding reliance on future provenance edges; this preserves deterministic acceptance and irreversible state change<cite id="3f93480a-0">Provenance can be stored in blocks under a Provenance Blockchain and retrieved via contracts to decide access and auditing</cite><cite id="3f93480a-2">Auditors validate using receipts; trusted generation and integrity/availability mechanisms reduce forgeability</cite>. 
- Use trusted generation to bound incompleteness: tie provenance creation to tamper-evident hardware or secure enclaves and encode constraints so that necessary edges exist before execution, limiting late-binding validation to read-only queries<cite id="3f93480a-2">Prov-Trust leverages SGX to provide trustworthy provenance data; unforgeability and tamper evidence are enforced to ensure integrity and availability</cite>. 
- Encode validation as monotone, conservative filters: accept only if all qualified provenance attributes are satisfied and remain satisfied under future graph completions; otherwise delay acceptance or use atomic cross-contract channels to ensure at-least-once, order-preserving validation before commit; this preserves uniqueness and liveness at the cost of latency and potential retries<cite id="cbb6ff9b-1">Qualified terms provide additional attributes to binary relations (e.g., plan) and PROV is retrospective, implying conservative acceptance requires accounting for future evidence</cite><cite id="3f93480a-0">Applications can choose granularity and timing of provenance publication, enabling staged validation that waits for necessary facts</cite>. 
- Formalize governance semantics at protocol level: define stable, versioned provenance ontologies and acceptance predicates in upgrade-protected modules; prohibit retroactive predicate flips that would invalidate prior transactions, aligning with consensus finality expectations<cite id="d0d1f706-3">Ontology of governance at protocol level, derived from analyzing The DAO, suggests encoding stable governance semantics to avoid non-terminating behavior</cite>.

6) Summary: violation pathways and alignment
- The core violations are: nondeterministic acceptance due to incomplete or evolving provenance graphs, integrity loss from retroactive evidence flips, and liveness loss from retries and reorgs when uncertainty persists; these arise because PROV-O is retrospective and contracts depend on facts that unfold asynchronously across validators and chains<cite id="cbb6ff9b-1">PROV is a-posteriori; provenance logs describe steps that happened, and qualified/expanded relations capture details that unfold over time</cite><cite id="3f93480a-0">Contract-triggered provenance publication/retrieval depends on developer-chosen granularity and network timing, creating legitimate incompleteness at transaction time</cite><cite id="3f93480a-2">Contract-mediated validation and voting mechanisms can change acceptance over time, enabling rollbacks or rejections of previously accepted outcomes</cite>. 
- Designs that align with finality enforce on-chain, tamper-evident provenance receipts visible to validators at commit; use conservative, monotone acceptance filters with explicit deadlines; and freeze semantics of acceptance predicates at protocol level so that “final” outcomes remain uniquely determinable and irreversible under known provenance semantics<cite id="3f93480a-2">On-chain receipts and trusted generation support unforgeability, enabling deterministic, tamper-evident validation</cite><cite id="cbb6ff9b-1">Qualified, retrospective PROV patterns require conservative acceptance to account for evidence completeness</cite><cite id="d0d1f706-3">Protocol-level governance ontologies aim to prevent non-terminating workflows by stabilizing semantics</cite>. 
</answer>

Title: Towards a Blockchain-based Architecture for Data Provenance Management in the Internet of Things
Snippet: This section describes the proposed architecture aiming to maintain provenance records, based on a blockchain infrastructure, and also provides two examples of its application. 

The concepts of an IoT architecture with data provenance support [Hu et al. 2020] are presented in Figure 1. The architecture we propose is located in the Middleware Layer and assumes that the other layers are defined and fully functioning. • Rest API: API designed to mediate the requests between the IoT Application and the smart contracts. It provides the IoT Application with operations to publish or to query the provenance data of a given object (thing) in the Provenance Blockchain. 

• Publish Provenance Smart Contract: smart contract triggered by the Rest API, responsible for publishing provenance data to the Provenance Blockchain. • Retrieve Provenance Smart Contract: smart contract triggered by Rest API, responsible for browsing the Provenance Blockchain for provenance data, based on the given search criteria, and returning it to the Rest API, which in turn forwards it to the IoT Application. • Provenance Blockchain: blockchain infrastructure where provenance data is stored in the form of blocks, following the W3C PROV standard. 

The proposed architecture aims to facilitate the management of provenance data for the IoT application developer. Therefore, the developer can simply perform calls to the Rest API in order to publish or retrieve provenance data about a given object (thing) that is stored in the Provenance Blockchain. It remains with the developer to decide the level of granularity of the provenance that will be maintained (i.e., which provenance data will be recorded and how often), as well as its purpose, which can be, for instance, to enable auditing over the application in case of failures or abnormal behavior, to ensure the reliability of the objects and their produced data, or to maintain access control over the information generated by the application.

Title: Security, Performance, and Applications of Smart Contracts: A Systematic Survey
Snippet: Kim and Laskowski [18] investigate applying ontologies for supply chain provenance. The study explains how to apply TOVE traceability ontologies in blockchain to enhance the blockchain provenance tracking by translating ontologies representation to Solidity smart contracts. Formal ontology axioms represented in first-order logic convert into Ethereum smart contract to generate traces related to intended physical goods. Figurili et al. [19] also implemented a blockchain application using Azure blockchain workbench to trace woods from standing trees to final products in order to fight against fraud. The data captured by RFID sensor devices adjust to respective smart contract and record on the blockchain and then become accessible for different parties to trace the history.

Title: Prov-Trust: Towards a Trustworthy SGX-based Data Provenance System
Snippet: The provenance data are stored in transactions that are broadcasted to the core of blockchain network created by a specific set of validating virtual machines. Similar to Provchain solution, the provenance auditor validates the data using the transactions receipts. SmartProvenance (Ramachandran and Kantarcioglu, 2018) applies Ethereum Smart Contracts to provide data provenance. SmartProvenance is based on two smart contracts, namely Document Tracker contract and Vote contract. The Document Tracker smart contract is used to monitor the operations performed over a given document while the vote contract specifies the voting protocol. A voting process is used to validate every provenance change event. 

These solutions do not address a trusted generation of the provenance data, yet unforgeability is a security requirement that needs to be achieved while generating and storing provenance data. The unforgeability means that an adversary cannot forge a valid provenance record either by modifying any existing one or directly introducing a new forged provenance record without being detected. Hence, unforgeability guarantees the tamper evidence (Asghar et al., 2012;Taha et al., 2015). A first attempt to use Trusted Platform Module to ensure trust in provenance generation had been introduced by Bock et al. (Böck et al., 2010). This solution presented a data provenance collection solution using a TPM chip and the AMD Secure Virtual Machine (SVM) technology. This solution has been enhanced further by Taha et al. (Taha et al., 2015) by adding the integrity and availability of the provenance data to the solution. 

In our proposed solution Prov-Trust, we leverage Blockchain technology and trusted hardware; the Intel SGX to provide trustworthy and secure provenance data.

Title: The security strength of Blockchain technology : A Survey Report
Snippet: The paper presents the blockchain architecture; how it can be used in provenance tracking. The study applies blockchain ontologies on knowledge traceability, knowledge provenance, and food provenance. Such ontologies can be applied in designing a blockchain system. The authors analyze the contribution of traceability ontology and how it can be applied smart contracts to enforce traceability constraints and execute a provenance trace in Ethereum blockchain platforms.

Only recently have researchers focused on conjoining the blockchain with ontologies [69,70]. One of the areas of investigation has concentrated in developing a characterization of blockchain concepts and technologies through ontologies. In [71], a theoretical contribution looking at the blockchain through an ontological approach has been provided. Title: A First Step in the Co-Evolution of Blockchain and Ontologies: Towards Engineering an Ontology of Governance at the Blockchain Protocol Level
Snippet: At the beginning of 2018, there is a growing belief that blockchain technologies constitute a revolutionary innovation in how we transfer value electronically. In that vein, blockchain may be a suitable complement to ontologies to truly achieve Tim Berners-Lee's vision of the semantic Web. We believe that if this complementarity is to be achieved blockchain and ontologies must co-evolve. In this paper, we focus on what and how to engineer artifacts (models, methods, designs, and implementations) for this co-evolution. 

Specifically, we posit that a pragmatic first step in co-evolving blockchain with ontologies is to encode ontology representations as meta-data tags to be embedded and instantiated in a smart contract at the blockchain protocol level. We further posit that an ontology representing governance structure is more likely to be adopted by smart contract writers than ontologies representing other domains. Finally, we analyze the smart contracts of the infamous The DAO experiment on Ethereum, from which we outline a conceptual design for a governance ontology at the blockchain protocol level. 

There is much more work to be done. As a start, the prototype design outlined in this paper must be implemented in Ethereum or another blockchain environment. Also, a more complete analysis of smart contract governance structures, including development of a more structured ontology remains to be done. This paper serves as an initial roadmap for engineering artifacts for blockchain/ontology co-evolution, and there are many design issues that need to be more fully explored. Title: Toward the Ontological Modeling of Smart Contracts: A Solidity Use Case
Snippet: One technique for representing knowledge is the use of ontologies, providing the ability to process semantics since ontologies encompass a representation, formal naming, and definition of categories, properties, and relations between concepts, data and entities that substantiate one, many or all domains of discourse. 

One domain of Knowledge Representation is programming languages, for which already exists ontologies that cover or model popular programming languages, such as Java and C. The use of Knowledge Representation applied to programming languages has improved current educational techniques and complemented some of these languages, providing additional parsers, code generators, or code validation. However, despite the popularity of smart contracts and the fact that they are also programs, and thus, expressed according to one programming language, there is no ontology oriented to represent smart contracts themselves. 

Smart contracts could benefit from the knowledge representation capabilities provided by ontologies in areas such as data validation, contract generation or extending the knowledge of a domain with other domains, inter alia. In this paper, an ontology for a smart contract language is presented, Solidity, which is the main smart contract language for one of the most relevant blockchain technologies, Ethereum [9], bringing knowledge representation for this language, linking the ontology to standard ontologies and making its knowledge reusable. Furthermore, this ontology has been evaluated with contracts already deployed in the Ethereum blockchain to assess its completeness. 

This work is organised as follows: Section II introduces the state of the art of smart contracts and ontologies. Then, Section III presents previous work done with ontologies and programming languages or smart contracts. Next, section IV details how the ontology was developed and explains the structure of the Solidity ontology. After that, Section V presents the evaluation method used and the results obtained. Finally, section VI recapitulates the conclusions obtained based on the results achieved and presents future lines of work.

snippet.text:
One technique for representing knowledge is the use of ontologies, providing the ability to process semantics since ontologies encompass a representation, formal naming, and definition of categories, properties, and relations between concepts, data and entities that substantiate one, many or all domains of discourse. 

One domain of Knowledge Representation is programming languages, for which already exists ontologies that cover or model popular programming languages, such as Java and C. The use of Knowledge Representation applied to programming languages has improved current educational techniques and complemented some of these languages, providing additional parsers, code generators, or code validation. However, despite the popularity of smart contracts and the fact that they are also programs, and thus, expressed according to one programming language, there is no ontology oriented to represent smart contracts themselves. 

Smart contracts could benefit from the knowledge representation capabilities provided by ontologies in areas such as data validation, contract generation or extending the knowledge of a domain with other domains, inter alia. In this paper, an ontology for a smart contract language is presented, Solidity, which is the main smart contract language for one of the most relevant blockchain technologies, Ethereum [9], bringing knowledge representation for this language, linking the ontology to standard ontologies and making its knowledge reusable. Furthermore, this ontology has been evaluated with contracts already deployed in the Ethereum blockchain to assess its completeness. 

This work is organised as follows: Section II introduces the state of the art of smart contracts and ontologies. Then, Section III presents previous work done with ontologies and programming languages or smart contracts. Next, section IV details how the ontology was developed and explains the structure of the Solidity ontology. After that, Section V presents the evaluation method used and the results obtained. Finally, section VI recapitulates the conclusions obtained based on the results achieved and presents future lines of work.

Snippet: The PROV specification is a recognized standard in the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) dedicated for the provenance interchange on the web [57]. In PROV (Figure 5), the provenance comes from the information about entities, activities, and people involved in producing a piece of data or thing [58]. The provenance information is often used to form assessments about the quality, reliability, or trustworthiness of data. In the PROV family of models, PROV-DM is the conceptual data model that presents the core model that constitutes the foundation for the W3C Provenance (PROV) family of specifications [59]. PROV-O is the PROV Ontology, an OWL2 ontology allowing the mapping of the PROV data model to RDF [60]. Three main components, prov:entity, prov:activity, and prov:agent, express, respectively, the data flow view, the process flow, and the responsibility view.

Title: Data Provenance
Snippet: Although there exist several provenance models used in specific settings promoted by different international initiatives, the main basic standard widely-used and referred to is the W3C's PROV recommendation 2 , which evolved from the Open Provenance Model (OPM). After three international workshops [1] on provenance standardisation, OPM was developed in 2010 and subsequently adopted by many workflow systems. PROV is very much influenced by OPM and was released as a standard by the W3C Provenance Working Group in April 2013. The W3C PROV Recommendation [2] consists of some constituent standards including for PROV XML 3 and PROV as an ontology for RDFbased data (PROV-O) 4 . 

The essential elements (see Fig. 1) of the PROV ontology are called Starting Point Terms and consist of three primary classes with unique and mandatory identifiers and nine properties to describe the relations between the classes. The three classes are prov:Entity which is the central concept and represents resources, prov:Activity representing actions performed upon entities, and prov:Agent representing persons or machines who bears some form of responsibility for an activity. The most important relationships are: used (an activity used some artefact), wasAssociatedWith (an agent participated in some activity), wasGeneratedBy (an activity generated an entity), wasDerivedFrom (an entity was derived from another entity), wasAttributedTo (an entity was attributed to an agent), actedOnBehalfOf (an agent acted on behalf of another agent) and wasInformedBy (an activity used an entity produced by another activity). Expanded terms are used to specialise agents and entities and to introduce time validity descriptions for activities. Qualified terms are used to provide additional attributes of the binary relations introducing so-called qualified patterns. In this way it is possible to add for example the concept 'plan', an association class, to describe more in detail how an activity was carried out. W3C PROV has primarily been designed to describe retrospective provenance (rprov) which refers to a-posteriori descriptions of provenance traces of data resources, i.e. provenance as an extended log of all the steps executed to generate the data entity.

In particular, we extended the three core concepts of PROV-O, namely "prov:Agent", "prov:Entity", "prov:Activity"; and its properties, namely "prov:wasDerivedFrom", "prov:wasGeneratedBy", and "prov:used". The namespace prov refers to "http://www.w3.org/ns/prov#". 

ProvCaRe Knowledge Repository: The provenance terms extracted by the ProvCaRe NLP pipeline is currently stored in the ProvCaRe knowledge repository as set of three related provenance terms (for a detailed description of the NLP pipeline, we refer to [23]). [20] as "hypertension status of participants", "was ascertained at", "second follow-up exam" in the ProvCaRe knowledge repository. Snippet: The specifications define a data model and an OWL ontology, along with a number of serializations for representing aspects of provenance. The term provenance, as understood in these specifications, refers to information about entities, activities, and people involved in producing a piece of data or thing, which can be used to form assessments about its quality, reliability or trustworthiness (PROV-Overview [w3c12]). The specifications include a combination of W3C Recommendation and Note documents. Recommendation documents include (i) the main PROV data model specification (PROV-DM [MMB + 12]), with an associated set of constraints and inference rules (PROV-CONSTRAINTS [CMM12]); (ii) an OWL ontology that allows a mapping of the data model to RDF (PROV-O [LSM + 12]), and (iii) a notation for PROV with a relational-like syntax, aimed at human consumption (PROV-N [MMCSR12]). All other documents are Notes. These include PROV-XML, which defines a XSD schema for XML serialization [pro13c]. PROV-AQ, the Provenance Access and Query document [MHS + 12], which defines a Web-compliant mechanism to associate a dataset to its provenance; PROV-DICTIONARY [pro13b], for expressing the provenance of data collections defined as sets of key-entity pairs; and PROV-DC [pro13a], which provides a mapping between PROV-O and Dublin Core Terms.

Snippet: Provenance information exists in many domain-specific standards 16,17 . There is also a World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) provenance interoperability standard called W3C PROV 18,19 . The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) is the main standards body for the World Wide Web, and has created many standards (called Recommendations) including HTML (used for web pages), RDF (a data model for descriptive information using subjectpredicate-object triples), and OWL, a language for defining ontologies for RDF data. In this context, "ontology" means a set of classes (defining kinds of things), properties (defining kinds of relationships between the things), and rules that impose constraints on the classes and properties, or define ways to infer new knowledge from existing facts. RDF and OWL are used to represent data in the Semantic Web / Linked Data settings, which have been proposed as ways to make data on the Web more machine-readable and more useful for automated analysis. 

The Provenance Interchange Working Group was active from 2011-2013 and produced several W3C Recommendations as well as a number of supporting W3C Notes (documents that support and explain standards, but do not themselves specify standard behaviour). The four main Recommendations are: 

• PROV-DM -which specifies the PROV Data Model, a collection of vocabulary terms used in the PROV standards and their intended meanings f • PROV-N -which specifies the PROV Notation (also called PROV-N), a serialization format for PROV information that is intended to be both human and machine readable g • PROV-O -which specifies a PROV Ontology (also called PROV-O), an OWL ontology that specifies basic constraints and usage for PROV Of these standards, PROV-DM and PROV-O are probably the most relevant for typical uses of provenance in the Semantic Web (that is, using RDF and OWL). Other formats for PROV based on XML and JSON have also been defined, but as supporting documents rather than formal Recommendations. The design rationale and lessons learned from the development of PROV are described by Moreau et al. 20 . Since PROV has now superseded earlier proposals, we do not go into further details about them.
