Expanded terms are used to specialise agents and entities and to introduce time validity descriptions for activities. Qualified terms are used to provide additional attributes of the binary relations introducing so-called qualified patterns. In this way it is possible to add for example the concept 'plan', an association class, to describe more in detail how an activity was carried out. W3C PROV has primarily been designed to describe retrospective provenance (rprov) which refers to a-posteriori descriptions of provenance traces of data resources, i.e. provenance as an extended log of all the steps executed to generate the data entity.

documents.title: Semantic Provenance Graph for Reproducibility of Biomedical Research Studies: Generating and Analyzing Graph Structures from Published Literature
documents.snippet:
The W3C PROV specifications consists of: (1) the core model called PROV-DM, which defines a common terminology system for representing interoperable provenance metadata [19]; (b) the PROV Ontology (PROV-O) that represents PROV-DM in the W3C Web Ontology Language (OWL2) [12; 16]; and a set of constraints (PROV-Constraints) to define valid forms of provenance conforming to the PROV specifications [4]. We extended PROV-O in the ProvCaRe project to model provenance terms associated with biomedical research studies. In particular, we extended the three core concepts of PROV-O, namely "prov:Agent", "prov:Entity", "prov:Activity"; and its properties, namely "prov:wasDerivedFrom", "prov:wasGeneratedBy", and "prov:used". The namespace prov refers to "http://www.w3.org/ns/prov#". 

ProvCaRe Knowledge Repository: The provenance terms extracted by the ProvCaRe NLP pipeline is currently stored in the ProvCaRe knowledge repository as set of three related provenance terms (for a detailed description of the NLP pipeline, we refer to [23]). For example, we stored provenance terms extracted from an article describing study on sleepdisordered breathing and hypertension by O'Connor et al. [20] as "hypertension status of participants", "was ascertained at", "second follow-up exam" in the ProvCaRe knowledge repository. However, this representation of provenance metadata has some limitations, for example (1) it is verbose (making it difficult to query efficiently); and (2) it cannot be modeled as a RDF graph structure. Given a user query, "How was the hypertension status of participants determined in this research study?", the ProvCaRe query interface uses keyword-based matching together with ontology-based "expansion" of query expression for retrieving query results.

documents.title: The lifecycle of provenance metadata and its associated challenges and opportunities
documents.snippet: The specifications define a data model and an OWL ontology, along with a number of serializations for representing aspects of provenance. The term provenance, as understood in these specifications, refers to information about entities, activities, and people involved in producing a piece of data or thing, which can be used to form assessments about its quality, reliability or trustworthiness (PROV-Overview [w3c12]). The specifications include a combination of W3C Recommendation and Note documents. Recommendation documents include (i) the main PROV data model specification (PROV-DM [MMB + 12]), with an associated set of constraints and inference rules (PROV-CONSTRAINTS [CMM12]); (ii) an OWL ontology that allows a mapping of the data model to RDF (PROV-O [LSM + 12]), and (iii) a notation for PROV with a relational-like syntax, aimed at human consumption (PROV-N [MMCSR12]). All other documents are Notes. These include PROV-XML, which defines a XSD schema for XML serialization [pro13c]. PROV-AQ, the Provenance Access and Query document [MHS + 12], which defines a Web-compliant mechanism to associate a dataset to its provenance; PROV-DICTIONARY [pro13b], for expressing the provenance of data collections defined as sets of key-entity pairs; and PROV-DC [pro13a], which provides a mapping between PROV-O and Dublin Core Terms.

documents.title: Data provenance, curation and quality in metrology
documents.snippet:
Provenance information exists in many domain-specific standards 16,17 . There is also a World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) provenance interoperability standard called W3C PROV 18,19 . The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) is the main standards body for the World Wide Web, and has created many standards (called Recommendations) including HTML (used for web pages), RDF (a data model for descriptive information using subjectpredicate-object triples), and OWL, a language for defining ontologies for RDF data. In this context, "ontology" means a set of classes (defining kinds of things), properties (defining kinds of relationships between the things), and rules that impose constraints on the classes and properties, or define ways to infer new knowledge from existing facts. RDF and OWL are used to represent data in the Semantic Web / Linked Data settings, which have been proposed as ways to make data on the Web more machine-readable and more useful for automated analysis. 

The Provenance Interchange Working Group was active from 2011-2013 and produced several W3C Recommendations as well as a number of supporting W3C Notes (documents that support and explain standards, but do not themselves specify standard behaviour). The four main Recommendations are: 

• PROV-DM -which specifies the PROV Data Model, a collection of vocabulary terms used in the PROV standards and their intended meanings f • PROV-N -which specifies the PROV Notation (also called PROV-N), a serialization format for PROV information that is intended to be both human and machine readable g • PROV-O -which specifies a PROV Ontology (also called PROV-O), an OWL ontology that specifies basic constraints and usage for PROV Of these standards, PROV-DM and PROV-O are probably the most relevant for typical uses of provenance in the Semantic Web (that is, using RDF and OWL). Other formats for PROV based on XML and JSON have also been defined, but as supporting documents rather than formal Recommendations. The design rationale and lessons learned from the development of PROV are described by Moreau et al. 20 . Since PROV has now superseded earlier proposals, we do not go into further details about them.

judgment.criterion_reasoning:
The answer fails to satisfy the verification criterion in several critical ways:

1. **Missing PROV-O open-world semantics citation**: The criterion requires 'at least one source on PROV-O's open-world assumption or incomplete provenance validity.' While the answer extensively discusses PROV-O's retrospective nature and time-ordered completion [6], it never explicitly cites or explains PROV-O's open-world semantics—the fundamental assumption that absence of information does not imply falsity, and that provenance graphs can be legitimately incomplete yet valid. The retrospective nature mentioned is related but distinct from open-world semantics.

2. **Missing blockchain finality citation**: The criterion requires 'at least one source on blockchain finality/consensus requirements.' The answer discusses determinism, integrity, and liveness in section 3, but these claims are not supported by citations about blockchain consensus or finality. References [3], [4], and [9] cited in that section do not actually discuss consensus finality requirements—they discuss traceability constraints, voting protocols, and governance semantics, respectively.

3. **Incomplete explanation of core incompatibility**: While the answer does identify that incomplete provenance creates validation problems (section 4), it frames this primarily as a timing/asynchrony issue rather than the fundamental semantic incompatibility between open-world reasoning (where incomplete = valid) and closed-world blockchain validation (where validity must be definitively determinable). The answer says validators 'may not have seen' provenance edges, suggesting a network delay problem, rather than explaining that PROV-O semantically permits incomplete provenance to be valid while blockchain requires complete decidability.

4. **Missing explicit consequence articulation**: The criterion requires explanation of one of three specific consequences (reject incomplete provenance violating PROV-O; accept it but validity becomes time-dependent; or nodes disagree causing consensus failure). While section 4.1 touches on 'different outcomes across validators,' it doesn't cleanly identify which of the three pathways is occurring or frame it as a forced choice created by the semantic incompatibility.

5. **Proposed solutions without acknowledgment of decidability problem**: Section 5 proposes mitigations (receipts, trusted generation, monotone filters, governance semantics) but does not acknowledge that these 'merely document incompleteness but don't resolve the decidability problem'—the criterion explicitly requires this acknowledgment if solutions are proposed.
other_issues: Citation mismatch: Section 3 claims sources support consensus/finality requirements, but [3] discusses traceability ontologies, [4] discusses voting protocols for provenance validation, and [9] discusses governance semantics—none directly address blockchain consensus finality as a technical requirement.

Conceptual drift: The answer spends significant space on oracle problems, sensor delays, and governance failures (sections 4.2, 4.3) which are related but distinct issues. This dilutes focus from the core PROV-O open-world vs. blockchain closed-world incompatibility.
Missing key term: The phrase 'open-world assumption' or 'open-world semantics' never appears, despite being central to the criterion.

Over-reliance on retrospective framing: The answer repeatedly emphasizes PROV's 'retrospective' nature [6] as the source of incompleteness, but this is insufficient—PROV-O's open-world semantics mean provenance can be incomplete even when not retrospective (e.g., during live capture), and incomplete provenance is semantically valid under PROV-O.

Section 5 mitigations contradict PROV-O semantics: Proposals like 'accept only if all qualified provenance attributes are satisfied' and 'necessary edges exist before execution' directly require completeness, violating PROV-O's design principle that incomplete provenance can be valid. The answer does not acknowledge this tension.
Verbose structure obscures core argument: The six-section structure with extensive citations makes it difficult to identify the central incompatibility argument, which should be front and center.
judgment.summary: The answer demonstrates extensive research into PROV-O and blockchain-provenance integration but fundamentally fails the criterion by not citing PROV-O's open-world semantics or blockchain finality requirements, and by not clearly articulating the core semantic incompatibility. It discusses timing/asynchrony problems and proposes mitigations without acknowledging these don't resolve the decidability problem. The answer needed to explicitly state: PROV-O allows incomplete provenance to be valid (open-world), blockchain requires validity to be determinable at commit (closed-world), and this forces an impossible choice that breaks either PROV-O semantics or consensus finality.
